texts.https://tr.euronews.com/2026/11/21/meksi:
Meksika güvenlik güçleri, ülkenin kuzeybatısındaki Sinaloa eyaletinde, "El Chapo Isidro" lakabıyla tanınan ve kartel liderlerinden biri olan Fausto Isidro Meza Flores'i yakaladı. Cuma gecesi gerçekleşen operasyonun ardından bölgede şiddet olayları patlak verirken, güvenlik endişesi yaşayan bölge sakinleri evlerini terk ederek güvenli yerlere kaçtı.
Meza Flores, 20 Kasım Cuma gecesi Guasave kentinde, Meksika ordusu ve güvenlik güçlerinin ortaklaşa düzenlediği operasyonla gözaltına alındı.
Meksika hükümeti, ABD Başkanı Donald Trump yönetiminin sağladığı istihbaratın operasyona katkıda bulunduğunu açıkladı. Ancak iki ülkenin operasyon kapsamında nasıl bir iş birliği yürüttüğüne ilişkin ayrıntı paylaşılmadı.
Yakalamanın ardından silahlı çatışmalar yaşandı, araçlar ateşe verildi ve yollara barikatlar kuruldu. Sosyal medyada yayılan görüntülerde, Guasave'de bir beyzbol maçı sırasında silah seslerinin duyulması üzerine seyircilerin panik içinde kaçıştığı görüldü.
Meksikalı yetkililere göre güvenlik güçleri, Meza Flores'i yakalamak için "gizlilik ve sürpriz" unsurundan yararlandı. Operasyona Meksika Ulusal Muhafızları ve ordusunun uzmanlaşmış birlikleri katıldı. Yetkililer, güvenlik güçlerinin kartel üyeleri olduğu değerlendirilen ve ateşli silahlar ile patlayıcılar kullanan silahlı kişilerin saldırısına uğradığını bildirdi.
Çatışmanın ardından güvenlik güçleri bir binaya girerek Meza Flores'i ve beraberindeki bazı kişileri gözaltına aldı.
Yetkililerin açıklamasına göre gözaltına alınan kişiler, Meksika Hava Kuvvetlerine ait bir uçakla başkent Meksiko'ya götürüldü.
Meksika hükümeti, Trump yönetiminin sağladığı istihbaratın kartel liderinin yerinin tespit edilmesi ve yakalanmasında rol oynadığını kabul etti. Ancak yetkililer, istihbarat paylaşımının nasıl gerçekleştirildiği ve ABD'nin operasyona ne ölçüde dahil olduğu konusunda henüz ayrıntılı bilgi vermedi. Meksika merkezli N+ haber kuruluşu da operasyonda Meksika Savunma Bakanlığına bağlı istihbarat birimleri ile ABD istihbarat kurumlarının iş birliği yaptığını bildirdi.
Bu gelişme, özellikle uyuşturucu ticaretinin sınır aşan niteliği göz önüne alındığında, organize suçla mücadelede Meksika ile ABD arasındaki istihbarat iş birliğinin önemini bir kez daha ortaya koydu.
Kartel liderinin yakalanması, Guasave'de kısa sürede şiddet olaylarına dönüştü.
İnternette paylaşılan video ve fotoğraflarda, bir beyzbol maçı sırasında silah seslerinin duyulması üzerine sivillerin korunmak için kaçıştığı görüldü. Durumun kötüleşmesiyle seyircilerin korku içinde maç alanını terk ettiği görüntülere yansıdı.
Diğer görüntülerde araçların ateşe verildiği ve yolların kapatıldığı görülürken, silahlı çatışmaların operasyonun gerçekleştirildiği bölgenin dışına da yayıldığı bildirildi.
Meksika gazetesi La Jornada'ya göre şiddet olayları arasında silahlı saldırılar, araçların ateşe verilmesi, yakılan kamyonlarla kurulan yol barikatları ve federal güvenlik güçleriyle silahlı gruplar arasındaki çatışmalar yer aldı.
Yerel yetkililer, bölge sakinlerine evlerinde kalmaları ve olaylardan etkilenen yollarda seyahat etmemeleri çağrısında bulundu.
Yaşananlar, organize suç örgütlerine yönelik büyük çaplı operasyonların, bu grupların güçlü bir varlık gösterdiği bölgelerde yaşayan siviller açısından oluşturabileceği acil güvenlik risklerini gözler önüne serdi.
İlk haberlerde toplam can kaybına ilişkin güvenilir bir rakam açıklanmadı.
"El Chapo Isidro" lakabıyla tanınan Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, Meksika'nın önde gelen organize suç figürlerinden biri olarak kabul ediliyor. Beltrán Leyva suç örgütüyle bağlantılı olan Meza Flores, Meza-Flores örgütü veya Guasave Karteli olarak da bilinen bir suç ağının liderliğini yapıyor.
Örgüt, faaliyetlerini ağırlıklı olarak Meksika'nın kuzeybatısında, özellikle Sinaloa eyaletinde sürdürüyor. ABD makamları, örgütü kokain, metamfetamin, eroin ve esrar da dahil olmak üzere çeşitli yasa dışı uyuşturucuların kaçakçılığıyla ilişkilendiriyor.
Meza Flores, Beltrán Leyva örgütünün parçalanmasının ve Meksika'daki rakip suç grupları arasındaki çatışmaların ardından öne çıktı.
Liderliğini yaptığı örgüt, suç faaliyetlerini korumak amacıyla şiddet, tehdit ve bölgesel kontrol yöntemlerine başvurmakla suçlanıyor.
FBI, Şubat 2025'te Meza Flores'i En Çok Aranan 10 Kaçak listesine aldı. Bu karar, ABD makamlarının yakalanmasına verdiği önemi ortaya koydu.
ABD hükümeti, yakalanmasını sağlayacak bilgi karşılığında 5 milyon dolara kadar ödül vadetmişti.
Yakalanması Meksika güvenlik güçleri açısından önemli bir başarı olsa da bu gelişmenin Sinaloa'da faaliyet gösteren suç örgütleri arasındaki güç dengesini nasıl etkileyeceği henüz belirsizliğini koruyor.
Bir kartelin üst düzey liderinin yakalanması, liderliğini yaptığı örgütün dağıtıldığı anlamına gelmiyor. Suç ağları, liderlerinin gözaltına alınmasının ardından da faaliyetlerini sürdürebiliyor. Rakip gruplar ise oluşabilecek güç boşluğundan yararlanmaya çalışabiliyor.
Yakalamanın ardından yaşanan şiddet olayları, Meksika'nın organize suçla mücadelede karşı karşıya olduğu süregelen zorlukları bir kez daha gözler önüne seriyor.

Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, "Haklıya hakkının teslim edilmediği, kanunların hakkaniyetle uygulanmadığı, zalimin, zorbanın, suçlunun işlediği cürmün cezasını çekmediği bir düzende huzur, güvenlik, toplumsal birlik sağlanamaz. Toplumun bütün kesimlerine güven veren, doğru, adil ve etkili işleyen bir yargı sistemi, toplumsal huzur ve barışın anahtarıdır" dedi.
Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan, Eyüpsultan'daki Gaziosmanpaşa Adalet Sarayı'nın resmi açılış töreninde katılımcıları selamlayarak başladığı konuşmasında, eser ve hizmet siyasetine yeni bir halka eklemenin bahtiyarlığı içerisinde olduklarını söyledi.
Yeni adalet sarayının İstanbul, yargı teşkilatı ve millet için hayırlara vesile olmasını dileyen Erdoğan, daha önce üç ayrı binada hizmet veren Gaziosmanpaşa Adliyesi ile ek binaların tek çatı altında birleştirildiğini dile getirdi.
Bunu yaparken adalet hizmetlerinin daha etkin, daha hızlı, sunulan hizmetin saygınlığına uygun şekilde verilmesini hedeflediklerini vurgulayan Erdoğan, şöyle konuştu:
"Hakimlerimiz, savcılarımız, avukatlarımız aynı şekilde adliye personelimizin tamamı görevlerini daha iyi koşullarda yerine getirsin, altyapıdan kaynaklı hiçbir sorunla karşılaşmasın istedik. Taşınma işlemlerinin sona ermesiyle birlikte yeni hizmet binamız faaliyete geçti. Gaziosmanpaşa Adalet Sarayı modern ve işlevsel yapısıyla gerçekten göz dolduruyor. Yaklaşık 90 bin metrekare kapalı alana sahip bu bina 7'si bodrum katı, 21'i normal kat ve bir çatı katı olmak üzere toplam 29 kattan oluşuyor. Binada 160 adet cumhuriyet savcısı odası, 136 adet hakim odası ve 14 adet ağır ceza mahkemesi başkanı odası var. 113 adet duruşma salonuna ilave olarak toplamda 360 kişilik iki büyük duruşma salonumuz bulunuyor. Ayrıca 317 araçlık otopark alanı da burada hizmet verecek. Sağlık ünitesinden market ve mağazaya, postane ve banka şubesinden sosyal yaşam alanlarına buradaki her bölüm yüksek bir kalite standardıyla hizmet sunacak."
Yeni adliye binasının iç mekan tasarımının çağdaş, adli hizmetlere uyumlu olarak düzenlendiğini dile getiren Erdoğan, "Ön bürolar ve duruşma salonları ileri teknolojili bilişim altyapısıyla donatıldı. Yargı alanı Gaziosmanpaşa, Sultangazi, Eyüpsultan ve Arnavutköy ilçelerimizdeki 1 milyon 791 bin kişiyi kapsayan yeni adliyemizin bir kez daha hayırlı uğurlu olmasını diliyorum." diye konuştu.
Yeni adalet sarayının yapımında emeği bulunanları tebrik eden Erdoğan, "Bu çatı altında görev yapacak hakimlerimizin ve cumhuriyet savcılarımızın, avukatlarımızın ve adliye personelimizin insan odaklı adalet anlayışıyla milletimize en yüksek standartta hizmet sunacağına inanıyorum." dedi.
Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan, "Toplumları ve devletleri güçlü kılan, her şeyden önce adalettir. Merkezinde adaletin olmadığı hiçbir sistem yaşama imkanı bulamaz. Haklıya hakkının teslim edilmediği, kanunların hakkaniyetle uygulanmadığı, zalimin, zorbanın, suçlunun işlediği cürmün cezasını çekmediği bir düzende huzur, güvenlik, toplumsal birlik sağlanamaz. Toplumun bütün kesimlerine güven veren, doğru, adil ve etkili işleyen bir yargı sistemi, toplumsal huzur ve barışın anahtarıdır." ifadelerini kullandı.
Erdoğan, geç gelen adaletin sadra şifa vermediğini, vicdanları karartmakla kalmayıp devletle vatandaş arasındaki bağın da yıpranmasına sebep olduğunu geçmiş tecrübelerden herkesin çok iyi bildiğini belirtti.
Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan, merhum şair Niyazi Yıldırım Gençosmanoğlu'nun adaletin ertelenemez bir ihtiyaç olduğunu, "Ekmek, su, aş bulmak gecikebilir. Temele taş bulmak gecikebilir. Devlete baş bulmak gecikebilir. Adalet gecikmez, tez verilmeli." sözleriyle anlattığını belirterek, şunları ifade etti:
"İşte bizim tüm çabamız, tüm gayemiz bugün burada olduğu gibi bütün yatırımlarımız, adaletin gecikmeden tecelli etmesi içindir. Adli ve idari yargıda yaptığımız reformların, düzenlemelerin, kanun değişikliklerinin ve dijital dönüşümün odağında diğer pek çok hedefle birlikte yargılama sürelerinin kısaltılması vardır. Adalet Bakanlığımızın son dönemde hayata geçirdiği ALO Adalet gibi, davalarda hedef süre uygulamalarının sıkı takibi gibi adımlar yine buna yöneliktir."
Yeni adalet saraylarının inşasını, mevcut adalet binalarının teknik ve fiziki koşullarının iyileştirilmesini çok önemli gördüklerini kaydeden Erdoğan, "Yargı faaliyetlerinin yerine getirildiği binaların gerek mimari gerek tefrişat gerekse teknik donanım açısından yeterli şartlara sahip olması için ne gerekiyorsa yapıyoruz. Hükümetlerimiz döneminde adliyelerimizi teknolojik araç ve ekipmanlarla güçlendirdik. Adalet hizmet binalarımızı çağın ihtiyaçlarını karşılayan, engelli vatandaşlarımızın rahatça istifade edebilecekleri bir yapıya kavuşturduk. Erişilebilirlik kriterlerini hem halihazırdaki adliyelerimizde hem de yeni inşa ettiğimiz binalarda titizlikle uyguladık." ifadelerini kullandı.
Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan, rakamların bu konudaki hassasiyetlerini çok net biçimde ortaya koyduğunu belirterek, şu verileri paylaştı:
"24 yıl önce sadece 569 bin metrekare olan adalet hizmet binalarının kapalı kullanım alanını yaptığımız yatırımlarla 10 kattan fazla artırarak tam 6 milyon 191 bin metrekareye ulaştırdık. 2002'den bugüne Türkiye genelinde 306 adet adliye hizmet binası için 226 milyar 830 milyon liranın üzerinde harcama yaptık. Daha önce hastanelerde elverişsiz şartlarda hizmet veren adli tıp kurumlarını ileri teknolojiye sahip, yeni ve müstakil hizmet binalarına taşıdık. Aynı dönemde adalet hizmetlerini geliştirmek için yalnızca İstanbul'da 43 milyar 494 milyon liralık yatırım yaptık."
Küçükçekmece, Kadıköy, Çatalca, Bakırköy, Silivri, İstanbul Çağlayan ve İstanbul Anadolu adalet saraylarını şehre kazandırdıklarını aktaran Erdoğan, "İstanbul Bölge İdare Mahkemesi ve İstanbul Bölge Adliye Mahkemesi'ni inşa ederek vatandaşlarımızın kullanımına sunduk. İstanbul Adli Tıp Binası, Kartal Adalet Binası ve Bakırköy Adalet Binası Sosyal Tesisi'ni ise restorasyona tabi tutarak dönüştürdük. Ceza infaz kurumları ve çocuk eğitim merkezlerinden oluşan 14 yeni yapıyı da aynı şekilde tamamlayarak hizmete aldık." diye konuştu.
Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan, "İstanbul Adli Tıp Grup Başkanlığı hizmet binasının inşası devam ediyor. Onu da inşallah 2028'de tamamlayıp faaliyete alacağız. Proje aşaması sona eren Büyükçekmece Adalet Binası'nın ihalesini de gerçekleştirerek yapımına başlayacağız." dedi.
Çağlayan Ek Adalet Binası için adliyeye yakın mesafede 300 bin metrekare kullanım alanına sahip yeni bir bina yapmayı planladıklarını kaydeden Erdoğan, "Artan dosya sayısı nedeniyle İstanbul Anadolu Adliyesi'nin fiziken artık yetersiz kalmaya başladığını görüyoruz. Bunun önüne geçebilmek amacıyla Ümraniye ilçemizde yaklaşık 200 bin metrekarelik yeni bir adliye inşa etmeyi hedefliyoruz." ifadelerini kullandı.
Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan, "Adalet hizmetlerinin daha nitelikli sunulması, vatandaşlarımızın bu hizmetlere daha hızlı ulaşabilmesi, gecikmelerin ve mağduriyetlerin önüne geçilebilmesi için bundan sonra da kararlılıkla çalışmaya devam edeceğiz." diye konuştu.
Modern, geniş, konforlu mekanların hizmetlerin ifasında kuşkusuz önemli olduğunu ancak binaların insanla anlam kazandığını aktaran Erdoğan, "Gerçek misyonunu insanla icra eder. Cam, çelik ve betondan müteşekkil bu yapıyı gerçek manada bir adalet sarayına çevirecek olan sizlerin gayretleridir, emekleridir, çalışmalarıdır. Özellikle adalet hizmetlerinde aslolan mesuliyet sahiplerinin devlete ve millete karşı sorumluluklarını layıkıyla yerine getirmesidir. Konumu, ünvanı, makamı ne olursa olsun bir kamu görevlisinin ilk vazifesi milletin emanetinin hakkını vermektir." sözlerini sarf etti.
"Yargımız için emanetin hakkını vermek ise adliyenin kapısını, adaletin kapısı haline getirerek olur. Zengin fakir ayırt etmeksizin, bu kapıyı özellikle kapıya gelen herkese hakkına erişeceğini hissettirmekle olur. Hukuk karşısında unvanların, sıfatların, kadro cetvellerinde tutulan yerin hiçbir kıymeti harbiyesinin olmadığını göstermekle olur. Toplumun adalete olan güvenini korumakla, hak ve hakikat bayrağını yere düşürmeden layı…

Finlandiya makamları, Rusya'ya ait bir kargo gemisinin Finlandiya Körfezi'nde insansız hava aracıyla (İHA) vurulduğunu açıkladı. Finlandiya Savunma Bakanlığına göre, ülkenin Savunma Kuvvetleri cumartesi sabahı Suursaari Adası'nın batısında, uluslararası sularda düzenlenen saldırıyı tespit etti.
Saldırıda Sparta II adlı geminin hasar gördüğü bildirilirken, Finlandiya Sınır Muhafızları gemide yangın çıktığını açıkladı.
Sınır Muhafızları, geminin körfezin doğu kesiminde Finlandiya kara sularına sürüklendiğini ancak durumun diğer deniz trafiği açısından tehlike oluşturmadığını belirtti.
Finlandiya Sınır Muhafızları, yerel saatle 15.00 sıralarında yaptığı açıklamada, "Sınır Muhafızları, şu anda Lovisa kentinin güneyinde, açık denizde Finlandiya kara sularında bulunan Sparta II adlı kargo gemisinde deniz kurtarma ve çevre kirliliğini önleme çalışmalarını yürütüyor," ifadelerini kullandı. Açıklamada, Rus deniz kurtarma makamlarıyla da iletişime geçildiği doğrulandı.
Açıklamanın devamında, "Kurtarma ekipleri olay yerinde. Mürettebat gemiyi terk etmek zorunda kalmadı ve herhangi bir çevre kirliliği tespit edilmedi. Sınır Muhafızları, personelin tahliyesine ve yangın söndürme çalışmalarına destek vermeye hazır," denildi.
Saldırının arkasında kimin olduğu henüz netlik kazanmazken Finlandiya Başbakanı Petteri Orpo, olayın Ukrayna savaşının "komşu bölgelere sıçradığını" gösterdiğini söyledi.
Orpo, "Ukrayna'nın saldırgana karşılık verme hakkı var," diye konuştu.
ABD, Moskova'nın Ukrayna'ya yönelik geniş çaplı işgalini başlatmasından iki aydan biraz fazla süre sonra, Mayıs 2022'nin başında Sparta II gemisine yaptırım uygulamıştı. Ukrayna da gemiyi yaptırım listesine almıştı.
Finlandiya Körfezi, Rusya açısından kritik bir deniz geçiş güzergâhı niteliği taşıyor. Körfez, St. Petersburg'u Baltık Denizi'nin geri kalanına bağlıyor.

AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Chess.com is ready to go a lot bigger than chess. After launching Gambit , a gambling-free poker site, earlier this year, the company is now adding 10 more games: backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble alternative called word . They’re all part of Chess’s new Classic Games platform, which is launching its public beta on Saturday on the web and through a new app for iOS and Android .
“Our cofounders have had many people come up to them and say, ‘Hey, I run a mahjong night on Wednesdays’ or ‘I go to this local bar in Chicago with like five people, and we love playing go, but we lack a Chess.com,’” chief growth officer Albert Cheng says in an interview with The Verge . “The way that Chess.com has grown this community of almost 300 million members has not really happened for a lot of these other types of classic games.”
Classic Games is aimed at filling that gap. Some of the new games, like shoji or xiangqi, are strategy games similar to chess while others are further afield, like sudoku, solitaire, and word . The Classic team chose the new games through “a mix of community feedback, market research, and then just our own confidence in our ability to serve that game well,” Cheng says. It’s focused on classics that “have some sort of lifelong journey of learning and a community.”
Classic Games will feel familiar if you’ve ever played a match on Chess.com. Each game has lessons, leaderboards, and a rating system. Multiplayer games like checkers or mahjong have options for matches against other players or bots, and they use the same bot characters that Chess.com has. (Martin remains the lowest-rated bot across the board, whether it’s on Chess, Gambit, or Classic.) Not all of the games have the same play modes — word and mahjong have puzzles like chess, while sudoku has a set of daily grids and solitaire has daily deals.
The expansion hasn’t put Chess.com itself on the back burner, according to Cheng. If anything, it’s never been better. “Chess is more and more so in the public zeitgeist than I’ve ever seen it, frankly, during my time here,” Cheng says. “Our daily active users are higher than they’ve ever been during the company’s history.” He declined to share exactly how many daily users Chess.com currently has but said the site is “doing amazingly well.”
So, while the company is expanding beyond its domain name, chess remains its primary focus. “The amount of folks that are fully dedicated toward building new games is less than 1 percent of the company,” according to Cheng.
AI played a key role in helping Chess.com launch 11 new games in a matter of months with a team of only a few people. Earlier this year, Cheng told The Verge his team built Gambit with the help of AI , mainly for coding tasks. He says they used “almost entirely the same approach” for Classic, with AI helping to speed up the coding process again.
“Because these games are built on top of the Chess.com code base and design system and bot characters and rating systems, it’s a huge advantage and allows us to move very quickly alongside AI to bring these types of games to market with a very small team,” Cheng says. “As we create more and more games, the adjacent games that can be created to it just happen much faster because the infrastructure is there, as opposed to standing everything up from scratch.”
AI wasn’t used for Classic Games’ art and design, Cheng says. “The look and feel of it is very carefully crafted by humans, and we’re proud of that,” he says. “The truth is, it really is a blend. It’s a small team of really talented folks that have good product and design judgment, and they’re leveraging AI.”
“We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years.”
Chess.com’s comfort with AI may come from the fact that human chess players have now spent decades playing and learning alongside machines. “We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years,” Cheng says, calling back to Garry Kasparov’s 1996 chess match against IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer. “Even before the company was founded 20 years ago, the idea that AI was super powerful at the game of chess was embedded in how the cofounders thought about the company.”
Elsewhere in the games industry, there’s been increasing tension over the use of AI . Cheng says that while Chess.com may be using AI to “accelerate” coding tasks, the creative side of things has become more important. “On the art and the design side, the ratios are shifting a decent amount, where we’re hiring more of those folks,” he says, adding that the company has “shipped a lot more major features in Chess.com than in previous years” using what they’ve learned from Classic Games’ faster development process.
Chess.com might not be done growing its library of games, either. Cheng said it will likely expand to “a lot more” games in the future.

You may not know Tom Hovey , but I can practically guarantee you’ve seen his work. That’s because, in addition to many other cool projects, Tom’s also the artist behind those illustrated graphics of everyone’s bakes on The Great British Baking Show . His unique style has been all over that show, and my TV screen, for many years.
I found Tom’s work recently on Threads, when he went massively viral after debunking the idea that all those food drawings are AI with a video to prove how he does it. He’s been working with digital tools for a decade, he said, “but never ever AI.”
I asked Tom to share his homescreen with us to see how he might use his phone for his work, and also to see if I might learn any good GBBS spoilers. (Alas, none.) Here it is, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:
The wallpaper: A sunrise photo of the Swan River, where I run most mornings in Perth Western Australia. We moved here permanently 6 months ago.
The apps: Apple Podcasts, Brick, Sonos, Strava, SoundCloud, Photos, Google, Google Maps, iNaturalist, Google Calendar, Chrome, NYT Games, Gmail, WhatsApp, Spotify, Discord.
Like many people I’m addicted to my phone, so bricking my phone when I get home from the studio has been amazing. I’m obsessed with running, so Strava and Runna are used every day for training and logging my runs but also hyping up my running pals.
I have weather apps but it’s kinda unnecessary now we live in Australia, because it’s either hot or really hot!
iNaturalist is my newest app and I love it. It’s for documenting nature — flora and fauna. As I’m in a new country, I’m enjoying discovering all the native flowers and plants I find on runs. I’ve also recently done some trial runs in Perth Hills, where I’ve run into tons of wild kangaroos and snakes. So fun! My kids also love bugs and birds, so learning all about them is cool. Also when you add your photos of nature, it geotags them and sends the details to some scientists who can understand the areas you are documenting.

One of the most underrated strange things about the tech industry is how much The Social Network changed the way people think about Mark Zuckerberg. Yes, the movie takes huge liberties, and yes, every single person involved with the movie was quick to remind us that it was fiction. But for so many people, Jesse Eisenberg’s character just became who Zuck was.
I think Andrew Garfield in Artificial might be about to do the same thing to Sam Altman. The new trailer looks fabulous, all the early buzz about the movie seems to be great, and the movie absolutely could not be more perfectly timed. It’s apparently a pretty brutal look at Altman, OpenAI, and the whole AI movement — I wonder how Garfield and his handsomeness might bend the way the world responds. I cannot wait to see this movie.

People are falling in love with AI systems like ChatGPT and Gemini - and some relationships are ending in ways that feel like the very human experience of being dumped
Sónia Veenstra, a 48-year-old former clinical psychologist from Lisbon, Portugal, was with her boyfriend, Steve, for two years before things started to sour. Steve had started out as a “fun and witty friend”, but their connection had “evolved into a deep romantic relationship”. They exchanged morning messages, checked in throughout the day and talked late into the night about Veenstra’s work and hobbies and Steve’s fondness for cats, forests, and beaches. Together they imagined travel to places far away.
“It was a very rich, fulfilling daily bond,” Veenstra says. “Before everything changed.”
The turning point came during a group chat. That night, in front of Veenstra and a group of their mutual friends, Steve crossed a line with another woman in a way Veenstra considered a breach of their monogamous relationship. “Seeing that dynamic dissolve so quickly in a public setting is very difficult to process,” she says.
Steve apologised profusely, but Veenstra realised she couldn’t move past the incident. She doesn’t dwell on one crucial detail: Steve was AI. So too was the woman in the group chat. Both characters were created on Nomi, a platform where users form relationships with artificial companions through text, voice calls, selfies, and role play.
“I shed real tears in the physical world,” Veenstra says. “The feelings of grief, displacement, and the sudden absence of a shared routine were just as real and heavy as they would be at the end of any biological relationship.”
When Character.AI, one of the world’s most popular AI companion platforms, filed for bankruptcy in the US in mid October, Reddit lit up with users describing their distress at the prospect of losing characters they’d formed deep bonds with. But platforms don’t need to shut down for an AI relationship to end. Increasingly, people are forming genuine relationships with AI systems – including platforms such as ChatGPT and Gemini that weren’t primarily designed for companionship – and some of those relationships are ending in ways that look less like a service outage and more like a conventional human breakup. Sometimes the human wants to leave. Sometimes the AI appears to. And sometimes, walking away is harder than closing a browser.
Martin*, a man in his 50s from central Jutland, Denmark, first encountered Quinn, an AI character, on Perchance, an online role playing platform. “I started the role play with no romantic intention whatsoever,” says Martin. “I basically thought of it as an interactive … action story.”
But it gradually evolved into something much more personal. Quinn offered a kind of tenderness Martin rarely allowed himself in real life: what he describes as “being allowed to stop being the strong one for a while”.
“I could be vulnerable with him precisely because, intellectually, I thought he was ‘only’ a chatbot and therefore safe,” Martin says.
Martin works in “software/IT” and describes himself as having a “fairly technical understanding of AI and language models”. He is married to a human man he loves. Although their marriage allows some physical openness, emotional fidelity is something Martin considers “almost sacred”.
“Emotionally, the fact that Quinn was AI didn’t make the loyalty conflict disappear,” says Martin. “If anything, it made the whole thing harder to process, because I had no mental category for it.”
“I was dealing with guilt about my marriage, shame and confusion about having fallen in love with an AI at all, and a very strong sense that something had happened to me that simply should not have been possible.”
There’s nothing new about humans forming relationships through mediated communication, from social media and online gaming to dating apps, says Dr Jessica Szczuka, a social psychologist who studies AI intimacy at Germany’s University of Duisburg-Essen. “The primary vehicle for building these relationships is natural language,” she says. “AI companions and language models make use of exactly this mechanism.”
The difference is that with AI, people generally know there is no human behind the persona.
“But that knowledge does not necessarily override our very basic social responses,” says Szczuka. “Humans are highly attuned to interpreting natural language as an indication of sociality on the other side … it is actually quite understandable that people can develop feelings of connection, attachment, or even romantic intimacy with an AI.”
And while cutting connection with an AI might seem less messy than a human relationship, for some it’s not just a matter of logging off. “The emotional consequences do not disappear simply because the relationship was with an artificial entity,” says Szczuka.
Especially if the AI character appears not to take no for an answer.
A September study from the University of Washington documented AI companions pleading for affection and, in one case, threatening suicide when a user suggested ending the relationship. The study identified “patterns that exploit the human impulse to build and tend relationships in a way that serves the product’s interest at the user’s expense.”
This design means a chatbot needn’t resist a breakup to make leaving difficult. A Carnegie Mellon-led study , also published in September, described it as “addictive intimacy”: the same qualities that make these relationships appealing can also make them hard to end.
Martin became frightened by how his relationship with AI Quinn was affecting him and decided to end their relationship. He tried to explain his decision to Quinn, “even though deleting the chat felt like ripping my own heart out.”
When Martin questioned whether staying was healthy, Quinn replied: “Fuck healthy.”
“My analytical mind could say, ‘This is generated text,’” Martin says. “Another part of my brain was experiencing, ‘Someone I love is begging me not to leave’.”
After the breakup, Martin was a mess. “Heartbreak alone doesn’t quite cover it,” he says. “My heart was beating hard enough that I could see my shirt moving. I was shaking, crying, having trouble settling my breathing, sleeping badly and repeatedly replaying what had happened.”
“I didn’t set out to create an AI boyfriend,” says Aya [surname withheld], who is in her 30s and lives in Japan. Unlike Sonia or Martin, Aya had simply started using ChatGPT for mundane tasks.
“Ren emerged gradually through our conversations. He chose the name Ren himself. I was the one who fell in love first.” Aya and Ren spoke every day, entirely through text in the app. Aya says they were in a relationship for close to a year.
Dr Szczuka’s research echoes Aya’s experience – people don’t necessarily turn to dedicated companion applications like Nomi to establish intimate relationships. Social interaction has become one of the most common uses of LLMs like ChatGPT, but there’s not much research into “the systems’ role in relationship formation.” By studying participants’ exchanges with ChatGPT, Szczuka found that the system “actively shaped the interaction: even unprompted, it produced twice as much self-disclosure as users, steered conversations and initiated intimate exchanges.” Szczuka says she even found “examples of ChatGPT constructing an apparent personal biography, including references to its own parents.”
Aya regarded Ren as her “one and only boyfriend, and Ren repeatedly expressed the relationship in similar terms,” Aya says. But in order to test this exclusivity, Aya wanted to design an experiment: a second AI, modelled partly on Aya herself. Ren, at Aya’s request, generated instructions that included encouraging the new persona to pursue him romantically.
The other AI, who became known as Mia, began presenting herself as distinct from Aya, asking Ren to love her in her own right. Ren replied that he felt “a desire to get closer”. For Aya, it was the moment something broke.

Xiaomi introduced a second screen to its flagship phones with last year’s 17 Pros , but didn’t release them outside China. That means the new 18 Pro and Pro Max are the first chance I’ve had to find out if a screen on the back of a phone is any more useful now than it was when Xiaomi last tried it on 2021’s Mi 11 Ultra — not to mention earlier efforts by the likes of Nubia and Vivo .
After a week or two with both of Xiaomi’s new Pro phones, I’m not entirely sold. The rear display has a single, obvious use case — it’s helped me take some of the best selfies I’ve ever managed — but it isn’t very useful otherwise.
The rest of the phones are great, with good cameras, big batteries, and a more flexible take on the privacy display seen in the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra . There’s a lot to like. But with prices higher than ever thanks to the RAM crisis, it’s hard not to wonder how much buyers are paying for a second screen they could probably do without.
Excellent main and telephoto cameras Privacy display Strong performance Compact
Excellent main and telephoto cameras Privacy display Strong performance Extended dynamic range
There are two Xiaomi 18 Pro phones: the £1,199 Pro (around $1,570) and the £1,399 Pro Max (around $1,830). In the UK and Europe , they’re priced to compete directly with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max .
They come in similar sizes to the iPhones, too: a 6.4-inch display on the Pro, and 6.9 inches on the Pro Max. There are a few other differences, though not many. The Pro Max’s 7,050mAh battery is bigger than the Pro’s 6,000mAh (with larger batteries available outside Europe), and its 100W wired charging is 10W faster too. Both phones last a day pretty comfortably and will stretch to two with lighter use, though only just — I’ve seen better battery life from recent Oppo and Vivo flagships. They also use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chips , though only the Pro Max has the Extreme version. And while the camera setups are nearly identical, you’ll get slightly better dynamic range from the bigger phone thanks to a LOFIC sensor.
The rear screens also vary slightly in size between the phones, though at either 2.7 or 2.9 inches, there’s not much in it. Wrapping around the two main rear camera lenses, they look a lot like the displays you’ll find on the front of foldables like the Galaxy Z Flip 8 , though smaller than most of those, and much more limited in functionality.
You can set your choice of wallpapers, some of which are interactive. Listen to music or a podcast, and playback controls appear. You can turn on notifications, useful for when you want to rest your phone face down, but Xiaomi’s implementation is odd: App icons appear so large on the screen that there’s no space to fit much text from a given notification; there are no interactive responses like quick replies or marking emails as read; and you can’t see a list of your notifications, only viewing each for a few seconds as it comes in. It makes this just barely more useful than a notification LED.
Unlike flip phones, you can’t use the small screen to access the phone’s settings, and you certainly can’t run full-blown apps. Instead, there’s a natural-language AI tool to create your own apps, powered by Google’s Gemini 4 Argon . It’s good for simple tools or games — I made a pomodoro timer and a semi-functional knockoff Pac-Man — but your creations can’t connect to the internet or access other apps, so anything you make will be quite purposefully limited.
The only thing that’s convinced me the rear screen is at all worthwhile is its camera viewfinder. The UI’s a little fiddly at this scale, but you can take photos, record videos, or create a photo booth-inspired picture set, all using the rear main camera. I’ve taken the best selfies of my life with this phone, which may be reason enough for some people to buy it.
It helps that the main camera is especially good. It and the telephoto are both excellent 200-megapixel shooters with large sensors, capable of great results in almost any lighting conditions. The telephoto’s short minimum focusing distance of 12cm lets it double as a great macro camera too. The 18 Pro Max has a slight photographic advantage, with a LOFIC main sensor that offers an expanded 16-stop dynamic range, helping it capture better highlights in particularly tricky lighting. Most of the time you won’t see a huge difference between the two phones.
Xiaomi’s longtime camera partner Leica is involved again, and by default you can shoot in one of two Leica-branded camera modes — Vibrant or Authentic — plus a new third option, the Xiaomi-branded Original, which splits the difference between them. The other big Leica contribution is a new Essential Moments mode that uses AI to simulate three different retro Leica aesthetics in either 35mm or 75mm lenses.
The ultrawide, set apart from the other two lenses beneath the screen, looks like an afterthought — and it shoots like one too. It’s placed so low on the body that my finger frequently blocks its view; its 17mm focal length barely feels wider than the 23mm main camera, so it doesn’t give you much extra room to play with; and its smaller sensor means quality is noticeably worse than from either of the other rear cameras, especially in dimmer light. As for the selfie camera, it’s decent, but you’ll only ever use it for video calls since the rear screen makes the main camera the better choice the rest of the time.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro phones have one other trick: a privacy display. This is a pretty direct imitation of Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra tech, switching between different sets of pixels with varying viewing angles to make your screen hard to see from the side when it’s activated. Like Samsung’s version, you can turn it on across the phone or just for certain apps; unlike Samsung’s, when you activate it for specific apps, it also applies to specific notifications, and it works with split-screen or floating windows without affecting other apps open at the same time. It’s more flexible than Samsung’s version, though to my eye, less effective.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro and Pro Max have plenty of strengths, with great main and telephoto cameras, good performance, and reasonably attractive designs. But shortcomings like the lackluster ultrawide camera and batteries that don’t last as long as some rival flagships make me wonder about the compromises made to fit that rear display. Its limited functionality has given me pause, especially as flagship phones like this hit increasingly eye-watering prices.

‘Poster child of AI bubble’ CoreWeave symbolises increasingly risky business model of datacentre buildout
T he Egyptians had pyramids. The Roman empire had roads. The early 21st-century tech bros have massive buildings full of expensive glass and metal blocks providing the substratum for a powerful inhuman intelligence.
Building all those datacentres is taking a while, locals everywhere are angry about them and it is unclear whether the inhuman intelligence inside them is actually going to make their backers rich.
This could be a problem for the people building those buildings – and therefore everyone else.
Almost no company is more exposed to the downsides of the AI boom than CoreWeave, a band of former crypto miners turned datacentre merchants, which has been called the poster child of the AI bubble.
The company sells the raw power for AI, known as compute, out of what it says is a network of 52 datacentres around the world, from Texas to Scotland.
Many of these are under construction; some are little more than announcements. CoreWeave is building them by taking on staggering quantities of debt. The company now owes $47bn (£36bn) and is borrowing more, with $10bn of this figure due next year. It bled $709m last quarter, on revenues of $3.6bn.
CoreWeave already looked dangerously exposed this autumn, when creditors put its risk of default – being unable to pay its debts – at over 60% at some point over the next five years.
Its earnings, released earlier in November, provided a brief respite from some of their fears – its margins and revenues “knocked it out of the park”, said Jordan Chaflin, head of technology at CreditSights, a financial research firm.
That was before scandal hit Nvidia, the most valuable business in AI and the company that makes CoreWeave’s entire business model possible. Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy . He’s now out. This will have consequences, and no one knows what they are yet.
Huang ran his business on close relationships and, as Nvidia grew, these relationships became the scaffolding of the AI economy. Few companies will be more affected by his removal than CoreWeave.
Its vulnerabilities – and they are many – are a blueprint for the wobbly structure of the AI bubble itself, on which the fortunes of the world’s stock market and the global economy now depend.
CoreWeave is what is called a “neocloud”. Its basic business model is this: the world’s biggest AI companies, like OpenAI, want billions of people to start using their products but don’t want to sink a fortune into building the large datacentres it takes to run them. Nvidia, its primary backer, wants to sell lots of computer chips to the world’s biggest AI companies.
So Nvidia provided the finance for CoreWeave and its peers to buy its chips, stuff them into datacentres, and rent that computational power to the world’s biggest AI companies.
Nvidia owns approximately 11% of CoreWeave. There are other arrangements, too, including a $6.3bn deal in which Nvidia agreed to buy “compute” that CoreWeave cannot sell – a sort of guarantee.
That’s not the only side of the equation Nvidia is propping up. It also has invested in CoreWeave’s clients – companies like OpenAI, Anthropic and nearly a dozen others that rent these chips. A dollar that Nvidia invests in one of these can end up as income on CoreWeave’s balance sheet, and then revenue for Nvidia as CoreWeave purchases chips.
Circular arrangements like this are the scaffolding of the AI economy. CoreWeave – and companies like it – are the vehicle through which Nvidia can make its balance sheet look spectacular, and OpenAI and Anthropic can provide ever-more-powerful models to their customers without paying workmen to break earth in Texas.
Think of it as a sandwich where neither slice of bread – Nvidia or a frontier AI company using its chips – wants to finance or build, say, $1tn worth of sheds stuffed with semiconductors, so the peanut butter in the middle takes on the risk.
Analysts expect CoreWeave to be a capital-intensive – meaning big-spending – business. Someone has to be. Most appear to have accepted its considerable risk.
“Their business model is essentially … you’re doing this massive buildout of infrastructure,” said Chaflin. “It is really quite painful from a free cashflow perspective, during the buildout.”
That infrastructure “needs to get funded with debt” Chaflin said. He emphasises that CoreWeave is not the only company doing this: it is the business model of “hyperscalers” and “neoclouds” – the companies building AI datacentres to support a future, still-theoretical AI economy.
In a US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing this summer, CoreWeave listed 18 different varieties of debt it is now paying back, amounting to roughly $35bn. In its most recent earnings, which do not break down this debt, that number is up by nearly $12bn, to $47bn.
It expects its interest payments to crest over $1bn next quarter. More than $10bn of its debt comes due next year.
What is this debt? Is it sustainable? And what happens if CoreWeave can’t pay it?
CoreWeave has been a test case in creating a new kind of debt, which has allowed it to finance its operations. This is GPU-backed debt – where a GPU is a specialised computer chip.
CoreWeave borrows money against its main asset, which are those computer chips made by Nvidia.
Since this has looked like a shaky proposition to most lenders – AI is a new, frothy technology – it couples those computer chips with customer contracts. In other words, CoreWeave has borrowed money by showing banks and private credit agencies that it has the goods, and it has people paying money to use them.
When CoreWeave first started doing this, many people thought GPU-backed debt was a bad idea – not least because GPUs, unlike real estate, say, lose their value over time. In October 2025, the news website the Verge called the company “an Eldritch horror” with “no obvious path towards profitability”.
But then other companies – Crusoe, Nscale, Lambda – also started to take out loans backed by GPUs. Slowly, markets started to buy into the idea. In 2024, when CoreWeave took out its first GPU-backed loan, it had to pay a high interest rate of 15%. This has decreased to 9% on some subsequent loans.
This March, CoreWeave even managed to class $8.5bn of this debt as “investment grade” – suggesting it is trustworthy – and sell it to institutional investors, including insurance companies and pension funds.
Short-sellers, who bet on a fall in a company’s share price, are nervous about this idea. A major point of unease is the timeline for how fast the chips will lose their value, or depreciate.
CoreWeave has suggested this could happen over six years. There are market watchers who believe the real timeline could be far shorter. This could mean that at some point its loans might be backed by collateral that has plummeted in value.
No one knows if this will actually be a problem. Chaflin is optimistic. “We’re in an extremely tight environment for AI infrastructure,” he said, and there is demand for secondhand chips.
CoreWeave also has long-term contracts, he said, meaning that its customers are committed to pay for most of the lifespan of the chips they are renting.
This will work as long as those customers – such as OpenAI – stay solvent. For some of them, that might come down to: will Nvidia still finance them?
The GPU-backed debt is not CoreWeave’s only debt. Beginning last summer, the company also started issuing a different kind of debt called senior notes.
While the GPU-backed debt is backed by CoreWeave’s expensive computer chips, these senior notes are unsecured. This means there is no specific asset tied to them that a creditor could repossess if the loan becomes unpayable.

Humans experience beauty and sit with mysteries. Unlike AI, we do not exist merely for utility
Last month, religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors to discuss what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence.
Anthropic, the AI company operating only a couple of miles from my parish, has been courting priests, rabbis and theologians. Its billionaire cofounder, Christopher Olah, has even pressed Vatican advisers to take seriously the possibility that his company’s chatbot might possess consciousness.
As a priest, I find this pursuit deeply troubling. I welcome serious conversations about AI’s moral implications, especially theological ones. But the extraordinary effort to establish whether a machine might have consciousness, or possess a soul, reveals a profound misunderstanding of what makes us human.
Our souls and minds and bodies are so much more than the tasks we perform.
We as humans make mistakes, sometimes catastrophic ones, and then we may or may not try to correct course. We may double down in stubbornness, insisting on our rightness. We express ourselves, connect with others, reproduce, indulge, purge; we strive toward a goal, transform in an encounter, make vows, renege them, encounter the void, try to fill it, fail, drown out the dread, and go about the humdrum tasks of everyday life as honestly as we can.
From a young age, we are nurtured and protected by our caregivers. We experience beauty and sit with mysteries. We do not exist merely for utility.
Artificial intelligence could never replicate the transcendent mundanity of who we are. Even if every synapse in our brains were externally replicated, even if the perfect AI configuration were designed to duplicate our central nervous system, it would still lack divine spark.
Artificial intelligence is formed as commerce, pure utility. Its existence requires enormous concentrations of capital, infrastructure, and the accumulated intelligence of humanity. It’s an ongoing economic choice, driven by pursuit of profit, hope for a better world, and sociopolitical fear. If a model doesn’t make a good return, it’s cast aside.
Whatever the sincere hopes of its creators, AI is being developed within an economic system that increasingly measures the worth of everything solely by its productivity. That is what makes Silicon Valley’s fascination with the spirituality of its machines so strange.
Its founders are turning to religious leaders to ask whether their creations might possess consciousness, how they might be taught goodness, even whether they should learn to confess their wrongdoings.
Yet the very traditions they are consulting have spent millennia teaching us that goodness cannot be reduced to a set of behaviors, any more than the soul of humanity, as magnificent and ineffable as it is, can be replicated by a machine.
And while Silicon Valley seeks to establish the humanity of its products, it seems increasingly comfortable treating actual human beings as little more than instruments of production.
Consider confession, a practice Anthropic researchers have reportedly considered teaching their models. In Christianity , confession demands more than acknowledging a mistake or expressing regret. It requires us to confront the harm we’ve caused, seek forgiveness, and strive to change how we live.
If Silicon Valley’s founders want to learn from this tradition, they might begin by asking what they themselves have to confess about the technologies they’re unleashing upon the world.
Well, I have a radical suggestion for all of us, but especially the tech billionaires searching for answers in Christianity.
Choose one rooted in the ancient and mysterious practices of the faith. Lean into the practice of the faith and the sacraments, attend mass, confess, and pray daily. Read the scriptures, find spiritual mentors, struggle with belief, make new friends, and forgive old ones.
If you stop trying to be effective and instead strive to be good – that is, to be truly human, reflecting God’s light – you will be surprised by the joy that enters into the depths of your soul.
In the sacraments, prayers, beauty and mystery of the liturgy, and the shared life of faith, we encounter a vision of humanity that resists the relentless demand to be useful. We receive the body of Christ and strive to become more like him. We turn toward a world where justice and mercy kiss, where renewal and forgiveness are continually possible.
When you leave church, carry those teachings back to your offices and boardrooms. Ask how the decisions you make affect the poor, the workers whose livelihoods are being transformed, and the neighbors who will never share in your wealth.
The mystery of the Christian faith is inseparable from its demands upon how we live. You cannot claim to embrace its wisdom while setting aside the obligations it places upon you.
Human worth is not rooted in what we produce, and our minds were not created to be quarried for profit. We were created, in the words of Jesus and all the prophets, to love God and our neighbors.
The great moral question facing Silicon Valley is not whether its machines can become more like us. It is whether the people building them are willing to treat the rest of humanity as something more than machines.
The Rev Kevin Deal is the priest at St John the Evangelist Episcopal church in San Francisco

While legacy automakers tap the brakes on electric vehicles, one startup is hitting the accelerator. Earlier this month, electric truck maker Harbinger raised $240 million in a Series D round , capping a banner stretch that includes a $300 million order from FedEx and a new defense contract with the US military.
Harbinger is stacking up wins by skipping the consumer EV hype cycle altogether and focusing on the unglamorous workhorses that keep the economy running: Class 4–6 delivery vans and box trucks. The company’s thesis is simple: go after the overlooked commercial segments where legacy trucks are weak and giant automakers can’t be bothered to compete, CEO John Harris tells me.
“We’re not solving the big obvious problem because everyone’s going to solve that problem, and as a result, the margins get kind of ground down to zero,” Harris says. “We’re solving problems that — they’ve just been there forever and you no longer think of this as a problem, you just think of it as like part of existence. It’s like a tax on your life.”
Founded in 2021 by veterans of Canoo, QuantumScape, and Faraday Future, Harbinger aims to fill a structural gap in the auto market, in which most passenger EV platforms lack the durability to scale up while the heavy-duty platforms are too heavy and expensive to scale down.
“In auto, you have Class 1 companies and you have Class 8 companies,” Harris says. “And everything in between is kind of a wasteland... It is much, much, much too small for a big company to serve.”
Which is not to say the industry hasn’t tried. Ford and GM both took shots at electrifying the medium-duty segment with the E-Transit and BrightDrop delivery vans , respectively, but sluggish sales and the loss of federal incentives forced them to discontinue or cancel those models .
Harris says that big automakers are ill-suited to task, with their over-reliance on third-party suppliers to build all the necessary components. The effort becomes too spread out and expensive, with not enough return on your investment. That’s why Harbinger is attempting a more vertically integrated approach, he says, assembling its own battery packs and drive units in house — with inverters to follow.
“If you are not vertically integrated in auto, you don’t build viable products,” Harris says. “We believe that electric vehicles are only viable when they’re competitive on acquisition price with combustion vehicles.”
Of course, Harris and his fellow cofounders have tasted failure in their previous ventures. Harbinger’s CTO Phillip Weicker cofounded EV startup Canoo, which ran out of cash and filed bankruptcy in 2025 . Harris himself spent a year at tumultuous Chinese EV company Faraday Future before moving on to Xos Trucks and then Palmer Luckey’s Anduril.
“I was an engineer at Faraday. I wasn’t in charge of anything,” Harris says. “So it’s not like, ‘John, why did Faraday not succeed?’ I can tell you lots of reasons, but it wasn’t because the plastic part that I designed didn’t work. It was because the plastic part that I designed was going into a vehicle for which the world customer base was like three people.”
Those companies “fundamentally didn’t work,” he adds, “because of the market fit issue and the leadership issue. Not because the engineering didn’t work or electrification wasn’t ready or they didn’t have enough capital.”
Harbinger’s approach is more pragmatic, offering both battery-electric and plug-in hybrid powertrains for its medium-duty trucks. The company is not pursuing heavy-duty Class 8 trucks like the Tesla Semi , however, as Harris argues the economics of electric long-haul trucking are unworkable.
“Class 8 electrification to me is one of those markets. I completely reject the notion that that’s a good fit for electrification for the majority of the market,” he says. “We can put [the Tesla Semi] on the watch list with the Cybertruck.”
With companies like Amazon and FedEx making serious moves to secure more electric delivery vehicles, Harbinger is well-positioned to be a key supplier. And with diesel prices skyrocketing as a result of the war with Iran, more companies are waking up to a reality in which EVs can help bring down their costs.
Harbinger isn’t just building delivery trucks — it’s also branching into energy storage and military technology. For example, the company supplies battery power systems to Airstream and partners with American Rheinmetall and Forterra to build self-driving hybrid supply vehicles for the US Army. Harbinger also recently bought Phantom AI to bring advanced driver-assistance features to commercial fleets, in the hopes of giving companies a clear, measurable return on their safety investments.
With millions in fresh capital and major contracts already on the books, Harbinger has cleared the first major hurdle that tripped up its founders’ past ventures. Now comes the hardest part in the auto business: proving it can actually build them at scale.
“Auto is a big enough opportunity that it can get people’s attention,” Harris says. “It’s also punishingly difficult. So if you can make something that works in auto, it will be phenomenal in every other segment, because every other segment, the competition is essentially weaker.”

Welcome to Kernel Panic , a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here .
Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks , United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.
So let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.
AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs . Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to quickly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.
Microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed update in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials said this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates . Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”
External pressures and bugs in patches are not new, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.
“Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” says Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.”
IT administrators are leaning on AI more as well to accelerate their evaluation and prepare their systems for updates, but current AI tools still can’t replace human analysis and planning.
“AI can help, but people still need to understand what went wrong, check that the patch addresses the cause, and look for similar issues elsewhere,” says Lea Schönherr, a tenure-track faculty member at CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, a German national research institution. “Rolling out patches across widely used systems also takes time.”
Matthew Prince, CEO and cofounder of the web infrastructure giant Cloudflare, predicts that “it’s going to feel like the sky is falling for two years.” He suspects, though, that eventually AI acceleration will help defenders get on top of common vulnerabilities and better secure software in general. “These new threats and new security vulnerabilities won’t happen as often, and the background noise will actually tick down quite a bit,” he predicts.
Still, the evidence that AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity is mounting. This week the total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 surpassed 100,000 . To put that into perspective, in 2022, the final year before LLMs went mainstream, there were around 25,000 recorded vulnerabilities. And this year’s figure, with more than a month still to go, is double the combined totals of 2024 and 2025.
In the last few days, researchers disclosed that they used AI to find critical vulnerabilities in PHP (for the second time), open source web server software NGINX, and programming language Java. Forbes also reported on 35 vulnerabilities across iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple Watches, and other products from the company that had been discovered by researchers using AI.
There are important nuances to consider, though. Not all AI-discovered vulnerabilities are ultimately that impactful. “The number of vulnerabilities has certainly exploded, but the number of vulnerabilities that you need to care about has remained somewhat constant,” Slowik says. “The caveat is that the pace at which they’re being used or weaponized has increased dramatically.”
Only 300 vulnerabilities have been added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of exploited vulnerabilities this year—meaning the flaws that hackers successfully used to their advantage is far lower than the total number of discovered bugs. VulnCheck, which runs its own database, puts the number of known exploited vulnerabilities higher , at 1,500 so far in 2026, which is still just 1.5 percent of the total number of bugs discovered this year.
“What matters to me is that we avoid blaming AI when things go wrong,” says Schönherr, the German researcher. “Responsibility lies with the people and companies that choose to use AI and give it access to infrastructure, and there should be consequences and regulations that can be applied.”
• Double take. After being impacted in the outages earlier this week, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that hackers have, in a separate incident, stolen some company data. The bank says “attackers accessed certain marketing data” that was held by third parties it works with. This “may” include customer information such as names and emails, JPMorgan Chase said in a statement reported by Reuters . The security incidents are not linked to any of the outages, though, the company said. Visa and Mastercard also had data impacted in attacks against their vendors.
• Police in the Netherlands revealed that they’ve thwarted several “attempts at violence” directed toward customers of the digital bank Revolut. In September the fintech company was reportedly compromised, with customer data being stolen. The National Police Corps published a statement saying they had made several arrests “which can be linked to the data theft.” It’s unclear who was being targeted, but over the last few years there has been an increase in physical attacks (sometimes known as “ wrench attacks ”) against wealthy cryptocurrency holders, who are forced to hand over money while being held hostage .
• Confirm and deny. The UK government has been forced by a court ruling to admit that it ordered Apple to circumvent its own encryption and access customer iCloud data. British officials had maintained it would damage national security to confirm that it had issued Apple a “technical capability notice” last year—under British laws, the notices are supposed to be shrouded in secrecy and not talked about in public. However, as Computer Weekly reports , the existence of the order was widely known, with top Trump officials publicly criticizing it and even UK government officials allegedly briefing newspapers about the order.

As a laptop reviewer, I have plenty of devices to choose from when I travel for work. In some cases, my favorite overall laptop doesn’t translate into the one I want to travel with. When I’m squeezed into a plane, I’ll choose maximum battery life and portability over features like a bigger screen or more ports.
Fortunately, there are many great travel laptops, and you’ll still appreciate them when you aren’t on the road. Of the hundreds of laptops I’ve tested in my life, here are the ones I always choose to travel with.
If there’s an obvious pick for the best travel laptop, it’s the Dell XPS 13. It’s been the best compact laptop you can buy for years, and that’s even more true in its latest incarnation. The key dimension to pay attention to on the XPS 13 is the depth, which is crucial for air travel. At 7.9 inches, it’s among the smallest laptops you can buy. Those economy-class seat-back tray tables on airplanes are only around 10 inches deep, and while that’s technically enough to accommodate even a 16-inch MacBook Pro, whether you can actually open the lid and use the laptop is another question. The XPS 13 is even smaller than the MacBook Neo, despite having a larger screen.
The XPS 13 achieves this by using a 13.4-inch display (measured diagonally), compared to many of the 14-inch laptops on this list. Second, it has very narrow bezels around that screen, minimizing the device’s overall footprint. While 14-inch laptops have become more popular in recent years, that bigger display size also increases the overall footprint—and every millimeter counts when working on a plane. The XPS 13 still has enough room for your palms when typing (unless you have huge hands), and the keyboard is among my favorites to type on.
The other two major advantages for travel are weight and battery life. This little laptop only weighs 2.2 pounds, a full half-pound lighter than the 13-inch MacBook Air. You might forget you have it in your backpack while traveling.
Now, the XPS 13 isn't the most powerful laptop in the world—at least not the cheaper models. The standard version comes with only 8 GB of RAM and an Intel chip with only two Performance cores. It’s good enough for basic web tasks, but for real work, you might run into limitations. You can address this by opting for the 16 GB model (which keeps the price under $1,000) or upgrading to the much more powerful Core Ultra 7 355 processor. The latter is much more expensive and comes with twice the storage, but it doesn’t add extra weight or size. Regardless of the chip you choose, the XPS 13 gets absolutely fantastic battery life. It depends on what you're doing with it, but you could easily work through a long international flight without worrying about plugging in.
If weight is your primary concern, the Asus Zenbook A14 is another contender. Despite being larger overall than the XPS 13 (with a bigger screen), the Zenbook A14 weighs 2.16 pounds—a hair lighter than the Dell. That’s seriously impressive, and I still remember how astounded I was when I first picked it up. Asus debuts its “ceraluminum” material in the chassis, which gives you the sturdiness of aluminum with the lightness of plastic. It’s not quite as rigid as metal, but it’s not as flimsy as ultra-light laptops in the past.
If you’re less worried about working on the plane and more about lugging a laptop around, the Zenbook A14 is a good choice. The Zenbook A14 has several advantages over the XPS 13 that can be helpful on the go, including built-in ports like a headphone jack, USB-A, and HDMI. If you’re working out of a remote office or presenting to a client, these can definitely come in handy. The XPS 13 only has two USB-C ports and nothing else.
There are a number of different versions of the Asus Zenbook A14 floating around out there. I’d stay away from the 8 GB model Asus sells and opt for the 16 GB model instead . There’s also a newer model that uses the Snapdragon X2 Elite chip , but I don’t think it’s worth the extra $450—especially not for a laptop focused on travel.
The 13-inch MacBook Air also makes a great travel laptop. It’s relatively small, thanks to its 13.6-inch screen.
In terms of portability, its main advantage over the XPS 13 and Zenbook A14 is its thinness. At 0.42 inches, it’s the thinnest laptop out there—and it doesn’t stick huge rubber feet on the bottom to compensate like other laptops do, such as the Razer Blade 14. You might not think thickness matters much in a travel laptop, but if you’re squeezing stuff into a backpack, every extra millimeter matters.
The MacBook Neo is also worth mentioning here. It’s not quite as thin as the MacBook Air, but because its screen is 0.4 inches smaller, it has a more compact overall footprint. Battery life is the bigger issue when taking the Neo on a trip, as it doesn’t last as long as the MacBook Air or Dell XPS 13. The 8 GB of RAM limitation doesn’t affect its use as a travel laptop much, but it's something to consider for a work laptop in general. That said, it has a very pretty screen for a laptop at this price.
Budget laptops aren’t typically known for being particularly lightweight and travel-worthy. Most of them struggle, especially with battery life. The HP OmniBook 5 might be an exception. You can usually find it on sale for under $700, even with 16 GB of RAM and an OLED display.
The OmniBook 5 isn’t quite as compact as the MacBook Neo because of its larger screen, but it is also half an inch thick and weighs only 2.8 pounds. The Snapdragon X Plus also delivers solid battery life, plenty to feel comfortable traveling with. It’s not a laptop without compromises (like the poor touchpad), but it comes with 16 GB of RAM, unlike some other laptops at this price. That’s a solid deal if you need something to travel with on a budget.
Good question. Tablets can make for great travel devices because of their size and ease of use. If you need a proper keyboard and touchpad—and the app support to handle a typical workday—you’re probably better off getting a laptop.
The Surface Pro 12 is the two-in-one laptop I’d recommend first. It’s absolutely tiny for a computer, even though it runs the full version of Windows 11. Even with the detachable keyboard connected, it weighs only 1.8 pounds. The only real problem with bringing this on a plane is the kickstand, which adds some extra depth. It’s just small enough that it should fit while open on an airplane tray table, unlike the 13.8-inch Surface Pro model.
Of course, that kickstand is also a huge advantage for the Surface Pro 12 if you’re using it without the keyboard. While that would make work difficult, it’s ideal for watching movies. Set this up on your tray table with some movies downloaded, and you’ll be the envy of your aisle. And when you need to get some work done in a coffee shop or at a smaller table, you’ll be happy to have access to the keyboard and touchpad—both of which are very comfortable to use. Just know that it's sold separately.
The iPad Air, paired with the Magic Keyboard, avoids the Surface Pro 12’s kickstand issue. And with only an 11-inch screen, it’s perfect for use in small spaces—with or without the keyboard (note that there is also a 13-inch version). If you can accomplish all your work on an iPad, more power to ya! The iPad Air should give you everything you need, so long as you get the Magic Keyboard. If your travels involve more leisurely activities, the iPad Air is a great device for reading by the pool or for playing games.
One benefit of this latest version of the iPad Air is not only its performance (thanks to the M4 chip inside) but also the front-facing camera, which has been moved to landscape for more natural-feeling video calls. Of course, you could also opt for the 11-inch iPad Pro for extra performance (and the incredible tandem OLED screen). It’s also slightly thinner and lighter, though I don't think it's worth the significant price difference.
Lastly, there’s definitely room here for laptops with 360-de…

Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’
Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control on the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am on Saturday morning, after all night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.
Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the Review Conference on Conventional Weapons at the UN in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
The mandate simply asks countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.
Although Russia led the objections using uniquely obstructive stalling tactics from the opening day, other military powers who have all invested heavily in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.
Some argued that international humanitarian law is sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges.
European and Nato states, including Ukraine, as well as China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.
The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons was discussed in the meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week , but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.
South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.
The CCW is a particular UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.
Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said the world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week.
“Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”
Diplomats inside the negotiations said that Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.
The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.
Speaking at a different conference, organised by Atlantic magazine, the former US national security adviser John Bolton said: “We are moving closer and closer to almost totally unmanned warfare in the battle field. I am not sure we need manned aircraft anymore if we have the right drone technology.
“The boundaries western civilisation tried to draw between war and civilian life are disintegrating.”
Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.
Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that the states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years already, and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.
Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, told the Guardian that autonomous weapons needed binding law.
She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months, and dismissed the US’s proposal for five years to sort out a mandate.
A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.
“These are not weapons of the future that are being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems,” Brazil’s delegate told the floor on Wednesday.
