It’s mostly been the subject of Hollywood movies , but one day, an asteroid or comet could collide with Earth and cause serious damage. We don't have to look all that far back for an example. In 1908, in an incident now known as the “ Tunguska Event ,” a space rock, likely a few dozen meters wide, exploded over Siberia. Though scientists weren’t able to visit the site for another two decades, the landscape was still scarred from the explosion.
Astronomers predict that in mid-April 2029, the asteroid Apophis will fly by Earth. The 450-meter-wide body will miss us at a distance of only 19,000 miles. That’s about 12 times closer to us than the moon and much closer than many satellites . It will even be visible to the naked eye.
In the past few decades, there’s been enormous progress in making these kinds of predictions . As space probes deepen our knowledge of small bodies in the solar system, astronomers have increasingly reliable and detailed data for finding potentially hazardous asteroids. Our ability to respond to such a threat, however, is another story. This is the missing and extremely important link—planetary defense technolog y that could allow us to deflect a dangerous object in time.
In a sci-fi flick, such situations are often solved with a nuclear bomb. But in the real world, blowing up a big space rock into tiny bits is not ideal. Instead, it’s better to alter the asteroid's orbit . Everything in the vacuum of space is in motion. Our own planet travels about 20 miles every second. If the object hurtling towards us can be slowed down and thus reach the meeting point a little later, it will simply miss the Earth.
Four years ago, this was essentially what NASA tested on a pair of celestial bodies known as Didymos and Dimorphos. Astronomers at the Kitt Peak Observatory discovered Didymos, an asteroid measuring 780 meters across, 30 years ago. A few years later, Czech astronomer Petr Pravec observed that this asteroid had a “moonlet” orbiting it about every 12 hours. This smaller body , measuring about 151 meters in diameter, was then named Dimorphos.
The paired objects were a perfect testing ground for the kind of deflection a planetary defense system would involve. Locked in on these targets, NASA launched the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) in late 2021. Nearly a year later, the DART probe crashed into Dimorphos.
Scientists had hoped that the impact of the probe—which was barreling toward the asteroids at over 13,000 miles per hour—could shorten the period of the mini-moon's orbit by a minute or more. In the end, it was slowed down by 33 minutes. This major deviation was caused by the ejection of debris, leading to a much greater recoil than what was produced by the impact itself. In addition, the orbital speed of both asteroids around the sun also slowed. And in a sense, Dimorphos briefly became a comet —the debris released by the impact creating a long tail behind it.
But questions remain about the longer-term impacts of this test. In October 2024, the European Space Agency (ESA) sent off the space probe Hera to rendezvous with both asteroids. After a flyby of Mars , the probe began its arrival phase this past October. It took its first image about 800 miles away, and the first detailed image of Didymos was published in early November.
Now in their vicinity, Hera will study both bodies in depth. Though there’s much we can learn about asteroids by observing them from our planet, nothing can replace close-up exploration , and this will be the first time a binary asteroid system will be explored in detail. One of the mission's goals is to find out how such asteroid pairs form. Didymos is also interesting for its rapid rotation, turning once every 2.3 hours—placing it on the very edge of stability.
But of course, beyond this traditional astronomy research, which could also take place at another set of binary asteroids, Hera will investigate the consequences of the DART mission. This will include studying the impact site. Because there are so many knowns about the impact itself, scientists can also use this opportunity to understand craters more broadly, answering questions such as whether the strength of the material or gravity plays a more decisive role in crater formation.
Hera will also determine the exact mass of Dimorphos, an important detail in assessing the effectiveness of the DART mission as a test of planetary defense technology. The probe also contains a lidar instrument for mapping the asteroid's topography and instruments for investigating the chemical composition of the surface . Additionally, we can expect to see detailed images of the asteroids taken with a resolution of 1 meter per pixel.
The probe is also carrying two miniature, cube-shaped satellites, called “CubeSats” for short, which it will deploy in January 2027. In Earth’s orbit, CubeSats are often used for simple experiments, including student projects, and they can even be stacked together to create larger satellites .
Hera’s CubeSats, named Juventas and Milani, will attempt to land on the surface . Using radar capable of probing up to a depth of 100 meters, Juventas will focus on geophysical exploration of the asteroid Dimorphos. Additionally, a gravimeter on board will measure how the gravity on Dimorphos changes during its orbit due to the parent asteroid, Didymos. Meanwhile, Milani will carry out a detailed investigation of the asteroids’ surface composition and will search for traces of dust and the volatile substances contained within many space rocks .
According to current plans, this main phase of the Hera probe's mission is expected to last until the summer of next year, and findings from this probe will likely only become more relevant, not just as Apophis approaches, but even after it slings back into space . In the year 2000, we knew of only 300 near-Earth asteroids—those that approach Earth or directly cross its orbit. Today, we know of over 43,000.
This story originally appeared on WIRED Czech Republic and Slovakia and has been translated from Czech.

Black Friday is associated with deals on high-end electronics, but it's also one of the best times of the year to pick up some new home essentials. Tineco makes some fantastic cleaning gadgets, and right now, many of our WIRED-tested favorites are on sale for up to 60 percent off. I've rounded up the highlights below, and you can check out the full sale here .
We're covering tons of early Black Friday deals and will be ramping up our deals coverage throughout Cyber Monday.
The Tineco Pure One Station 5 is a very solid cordless vacuum . We like its self-emptying docking station that's easy to set up (no drilling or fancy installation required). There's a handy headlight that makes it easier to spot dirt and debris, and we like the large canister capacity. It performs better on hardwood than on carpet, though. This is the best price we've seen for it.
This carpet cleaner is on the heavy side, but it's one of our favorites, especially with its easy-to-rinse tanks for the dirty and clean water. There's a large LED screen that shows which cleaning mode you're in, and the drying mode gets everything dried off in a flash. It'll pull old stains from your carpet and even comes with an accessory for upholstery.
I haven't tested the newer version of this steam mop yet, but I've been testing models from other brands for an update to that buying guide , and this older Floor One S7 still holds up. It looks great on its docking station, and it cleans my floors efficiently without leaving behind too much water. It does struggle along baseboards, but I truthfully have yet to meet a steam mop that doesn't. It is easy to maneuver with its self-propulsion and also has a handy light that'll show you cleaning progress as you pass over an area. I like the built-in suction too, which means I don't have to use two gadgets to clean one floor.

I hate running out of power. Everybody does. While our gadgets have advanced in many ways, battery technology has been slow to improve. That’s why you’re looking to buy a power bank. A good portable charger is a handy backup that can keep your smartphone, tablet, and maybe even your laptop going for longer. I’ve been testing power banks for years. I’ve tested more than 100 portable chargers. But you only really need one or two.
Most folks should buy one of the first four power banks I recommend, but there are a few other unique use cases, so I’ve included a few extra options. Read the Best MagSafe/Qi2 Power Banks for more magnetic wireless chargers, and Best Laptop Power Banks or Best Portable Power Stations for more power.
Updated November 2026: I added power banks from Anker, Peak Design, Nitecore, and Iniu, removed some older devices, and updated links and prices.
This is the only power bank you need. Anker combines style and substance with this versatile power bank that packs a whopping 25,000-mAh capacity and is capable of delivering up to 165 watts to two devices (100 watts for a single device connected via USB-C). I love the rounded edges, the retractable, flat 2.3-foot USB-C cable up top, and the clever braided 1-foot USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop. It has a display to show the remaining battery, charging rate in and out, battery temperature, and health. It supports pass-through charging and takes around two hours to recharge.
OK, you don’t really need this many stats, but having a precise idea of how much power remains is useful and reassuring. I love the built-in cables, because they ensure you’re never caught without one. This is also below the limit for power banks on flights , so you can travel with it. Anker’s Laptop Power Bank fast-charged everything I tested it with, including multiple smartphones, an iPad, a Poco tablet, a MacBook Air, and a Chromebook. You can charge four devices simultaneously without any issues. After a year of use, mine still performs perfectly.
You don’t always need big capacity, and you don’t always have room for a big power bank. If you want something more portable, go for the Nimble Champ Pro. At 6.2 ounces, it’s one of the lightest on the market. It’s smaller than a deck of cards and can deliver 20 watts to charge two devices at once via a USB-C port on either end. It feels durable, comes in a snazzy new range of speckled color finishes, and has a bright lanyard loop that makes for easy carrying and helps you pick it out of your backpack. The Pro version is bigger but doubles the capacity (to 20,000 mAh) and has a similar design with two USB-C ports that go up to 65 watts. There’s also a smaller version with a 5,200-mAh capacity that tops out at 15 watts.
Another reason I like Nimble is its environmental efforts . Batteries are not environmentally benign. They use lithium, cobalt, and other rare metals whose supply chains are environmentally and socially questionable at best. But Nimble’s use of bioplastics and plastic-free minimal packaging at least reduces the environmental impact where it can be reduced. This version uses 90 percent recycled plastic (up 25 percent from the original) and comes in smaller plastic-free packaging. Nimble includes a 3.3-foot USB-C to USB-C cable in the box.
The original was the first Qi2 power bank I tested and was my top pick for quite a while, but this sequel is even better. The Qi2 wireless charging standard borrows elements of Apple’s MagSafe, enabling supported phones to connect with perfect alignment using a ring of magnets. Because it works with Apple's StandBy mode, you can stick Qi2 or MagSafe phones in portrait or landscape orientation.
Qi2 brings faster wireless charging rates of up to 25 watts, but it is also backward compatible, so older Qi devices can still charge (albeit more slowly). This compact portable charger has a handy kickstand, a two-way USB-C port on the left edge, and a power button with an LED display that can show remaining power as a percentage. It can also display charging time when plugged in, watts out, temperature, and battery health. Anker offers the device in a range of fun colors (I love the burgundy). Anker has added vents on top and bottom with a cooling fan you can turn off for silent mode. It is slimmer and lighter than the original and can charge faster, but it's also more expensive.
Despite a large capacity, it falls short of two full charges for your iPhone when charging wirelessly. You might squeeze out a little more if you plug in the short USB-C cable provided. It’s also quite bulky, but if you have an iPhone or another Qi2 phone, we recommend several slimmer alternatives in our Best Qi2 and MagSafe Power Banks guide .
Maybe you want a large-capacity power bank that can handle all your portable gadgets, but you’re tired of gray bricks. I am a sucker for Sharge’s transparent designs and cyberpunk aesthetic, but this prism-shaped power bank is more than just a pretty face. With a maximum output of 170 watts, a whopping 24,000-mAh capacity, and an IP66 rating for water resistance (fine in the rain, but best not to submerge), the Sharge 170 has form and function. The smart display shows battery life as a percentage, time remaining, and the input or output in watts. It supports many standards, including Power Delivery 3.1, Quick Charge 4.0, and PPS, and it fast-charged most of the devices I tested, including the iPhone 15 Pro, Pixel 8, Xiaomi 14 Ultra, and MacBook Air. You can simultaneously charge three devices at fast speeds.
The box includes a braided USB-C cable and a somewhat pointless wee velvety bag (does anyone use these?). It can recharge completely in an hour via USB-C at up to 140 watts (with the right cable and charger). I’ve tested some of Sharge’s newer power banks, but I still prefer the 170. The triangular design is unique and means the display is always angled perfectly to glance at. You are paying a premium for the aesthetic, but I’ve used mine often over the last few months. It’s built to last.
My Apple Watch usually makes it to bedtime, but for super busy days and overnight trips, it’s nice to have a power bank capable of charging it up. This Anker power bank has a handy pop-up Apple Watch charger that can deliver 5 watts and supports Nightstand mode. It also has a built-in USB-C cable and a USB-C port, so you can deliver up to 30 watts to your phone or another small device. A display lights up beneath the surface to show you the remaining power as a percentage, and the current charging rate. It’s nice and compact, with a generous 10,000-mAh battery capacity, and comes in black, white, green, or pink. Anker supplies stickers to stop your Apple Watch from sliding, but I didn’t find that to be a problem.
Innovative and genuinely useful, I love the Nimble SharePower , a 10,000-mAh, modular power bank that you can snap in half to get two separate, fully functional 5,000-mAh chargers. This clever design allows you to share power with friends and family. The two halves connect magnetically with tiny pogo pins (it’s satisfying to pull them apart and reconnect). One has a built-in USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop, and the other has a fold-out USB-C connector. Put them together, and the remaining power is split evenly between the two halves. My daughter pinched this soon after it arrived in my home because it enables her to share the power with her friends, and I’m having trouble getting it back.
There are so many portable chargers out there. Here are a few more I like that just missed out on a place above for one reason or another. We also have separate guides for the Best Laptop Power Banks , Best MagSafe Power Banks , and Best Portable Power Stations .

The current flagship television from Sony, the Bravia 9 II, is an RGB TV model (Sony calls it “True RGB”) that brings to life even the darkest scenes in Game of Thrones . Much brighter than the midrange Bravia 7 II , the 9 II's best qualities are related to its black levels, picture quality, and excellent viewing angles that allow me to see Jon Snow and the GoT dragons perfectly, even when I'm sitting off to the side.
This premium Sony television carries a premium price of $3,600 for the 65-inch model, but that’s still $1,400 less than the LG Micro RGB Evo , which retails for $5,000. I ended up preferring the overall picture quality of that LG model and some other OLED models, but—after my usual rigorous testing—I felt the Bravia 9 II came close to matching the high caliber of those other options. In fact, it’s just a notch or two lower than the absolute best television you might find.
The Sony Bravia 9 II is all black, sits on two feet, and includes four HDMI ports (only two are HDMI 2.1, though, which allows for higher-bandwidth streaming and sound at 48 Gbps). Setup was a breeze; Google TV was up and running in less than five minutes, which is an impressive feat, given that both Samsung and LG televisions typically add a few extra steps to the install process, such as authenticating your login (with Samsung) or relying on an app (with the LG ThinQ).
The premium Sony Bravia 9 II also offers exceptional sound. It includes two upfiring tweeters for more realistic Dolby Atmos than the Bravia 7 II, which lacks these extra channels. When I watched House of the Dragon , the room-filling audio made me feel like I was flying a dragon or piloting a ship.
Viewing angles on the Bravia 9 II are about the best I’ve seen on any television. I tested this element by camping out in a chair and playing video games off to the side, and there wasn’t a hint of screen glare. These perks are, again, a sign of its premium quality, verified through my usual benchmarks. Skin tones looked varied and vivid; one person had a little more red in her face than what I noticed on the LG Micro RGB Evo or the Samsung Micro RGB R95H .
In a demo-reel benchmark test I use for all televisions, I was shocked by the Bravia 9 II's stellar performance. I’ve watched the same short segment with a fence in front of a winter landscape countless times to test various models, but here, the green grass in the background looked supremely vivid and clear. It’s because the Bravia 9 II has such exceptional screen brightness, color accuracy, and absolutely no glare.
The Sony remote is just OK. I wish the Home button were centered; since it's not, I kept clicking the mic for the Google Gemini voicebot (which is in the center) by mistake. I prefer the bare-bones Samsung remote or the one included with an Apple TV 4K streaming device. Just give me a Netflix button and volume controls, and I’m good. Still, the layout of this remote mostly makes sense, and I like that it’s backlit.
The Bravia 9 II didn’t pass all of my tests for performance while I watched shows and movies, but it did allow me to tweak more settings than I’m used to. For example, the TV automatically calibrated colors and tones for Spider-Man: Brand New Day , but it still looked too dark. I was able to manually adjust the black level and used Vivid mode to make Spidey’s suit look extra red.
However, compared to the picture quality of an OLED like the Samsung S95H, the Bravia 9 II's deep blacks looked less realistic. That's because on OLED TVs, the LEDs can be turned off entirely. The Bravia 9 II performed OK for Toy Story 5 , but in darker scenes late in the film, I noticed the Samsung had inky blacks that reminded me of a high-end projector.
My main takeaway is that it's nice that you can tweak settings on the Bravia 9 II to great effect, thanks to an RGB panel that’s super-bright. The movies Awake and The Creator tested my patience a little in that regard. I adjusted the black level to precisely 61 (out of 100) and could then see faces, a predawn mountain scene, and a beach landing with better clarity. Knowing you can achieve those results is nice; actually doing it does take time.
While playing Resident Evil: Requiem to test brightness, picture quality, and latency, I confirmed that it's possible to adjust the black level to liven up dark scenes. I also noticed that the latency, at a 120-Hz refresh rate when I used one of the HDMI 2.1 ports, was almost nonexistent. That helped with every slight twitch when a seven-headed monster from the dark underworld of hell started attacking me.
Similar games, like Senua's Saga: Hellblade II , looked too gray and washed out on the midrange Bravia 7 II and some LED models I’ve tested. I also played End of Abyss , a game that takes place almost entirely in dark hallways, and the Bravia 9 II rendered those scenes with inky blacks—granted, not as black as an OLED would, but better than many LED TVs.
Bravia 9 II lived up to its flagship-quality promise for sportscasts, making my beloved Minnesota Vikings' purple jerseys look vivid and clear and the grass bright green—all without displaying any glare at all. News programs were bright, with strong color accuracy, but not oversaturated—a good compromise. In fact, it was so clear, I felt as if I could reach out to clip an MS Now analyst's nose hairs.
The Bravia 9 II is near the top of the leaderboard of the best televisions to buy right now. You'll just want to consider the technology it uses. RGB models use red, green, and blue LEDs to create realistic colors that, in theory, improve color accuracy and vividness. Unlike an OLED TV, an RGB TV still shines those LED colors through an LCD panel. So you have to pick your poison. The Bravia 9 II looked super bright and vivid, especially during NFL games. It’s just a hair less colorful and vivid compared to the LG Micro RGB Evo.
Knowing you can tweak the settings for the results you want and that anyone in your household will be able to see America’s Got Talent from any angle in the room is a major plus. But is the Sony Bravia 9 II worth $3,600 when so many TVs cost around $2,000? I would say it depends on what you watch. I want to see dragons at night and monsters in dark hallways, but for some animated shows, sports, and network TV, you might just want your device to work well, right out of the box, without worrying about cinematic quality. Yes, a flagship lets you do a lot more, but at a much steeper price.

Mexican security forces have captured notorious cartel leader Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, better known as ‘El Chapo Isidro’, in the north-western state of Sinaloa, triggering a wave of violence that sent residents fleeing for safety.
The arrest took place in Guasave on Friday night, 20 November, during an operation involving Mexican military and security forces. The Mexican government said intelligence provided by the administration of US President Donald Trump had contributed to the operation, although it has not disclosed precisely how the two countries co-operated.
The arrest was followed by armed confrontations, burning vehicles and roadblocks. Disturbing footage circulating on social media showed spectators fleeing in panic as gunfire interrupted a baseball match in Guasave.
According to Mexican authorities, security forces used what they described as ‘stealth and surprise’ to apprehend Meza Flores.
The operation involved specialist units from the Mexican National Guard and Army. Officials said their personnel came under attack from armed individuals using firearms and explosives, believed to be cartel operatives.
Following the exchange of fire, security forces entered a property and arrested Meza Flores, along with other individuals.
The detainees were subsequently evacuated aboard a Mexican Air Force aircraft to Mexico City, according to the authorities.
The Mexican government acknowledged that intelligence supplied by the Trump administration had played a role in locating and capturing the cartel leader. However, officials have so far provided few details about the intelligence-sharing arrangements or the extent of American involvement.
Mexican news outlet N+ also reported that intelligence agencies from Mexico's Defence Ministry and the United States had co-operated in the operation.
The development highlights the importance of intelligence cooperation between Mexico and the United States in tackling organised crime, particularly given the cross-border nature of the drug trade.
The arrest quickly turned into a night of violence in Guasave.
Videos and photographs shared online showed civilians running for cover as gunfire erupted during a baseball match. Spectators could be seen leaving the venue in fear as the situation deteriorated.
Other footage showed vehicles set alight and roads blocked, while armed confrontations reportedly spread beyond the immediate area of the operation.
According to Mexican newspaper La Jornada , the violence included shootings, vehicle fires, roadblocks involving burning lorries and clashes between federal forces and armed groups.
Local authorities urged residents to remain indoors and avoid travelling on affected roads.
The scenes illustrate the immediate risks that major operations against organised crime can pose to civilians living in areas where criminal groups maintain a strong presence.
No reliable overall casualty figure was established in the initial reports.
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as ‘El Chapo Isidro’, is considered one of Mexico's most significant organised-crime figures.
He is associated with the Beltrán Leyva criminal organisation and leads a network also known as the Meza-Flores organisation or the Guasave Cartel.
The group has operated primarily in north-western Mexico, particularly in Sinaloa, and has been linked by US authorities to the trafficking of several illegal drugs, including cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin and marijuana.
Meza Flores rose to prominence following the fragmentation of the Beltrán Leyva organisation and the wider conflicts between rival criminal factions in Mexico.
His organisation has been accused of using violence, intimidation and territorial control to protect its criminal activities.
In February 2025, the FBI placed Meza Flores on its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, underlining the importance US authorities attached to his capture.
The US government had offered a reward of up to US$5 million for information leading to his arrest.
Although the arrest is a major achievement for Mexican security forces, it remains to be seen how it will affect the balance of power between criminal organisations operating in Sinaloa.
The capture of a senior cartel figure does not necessarily mean the dismantling of the organisation he leads. Criminal networks can remain operational following the arrest of their leaders, while rival groups may attempt to exploit any resulting power vacuum.
The immediate unrest highlights the continuing challenges facing the country in its fight against organised crime.

Members of the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons fail to agree on swift adoption of legally binding rules.
The 128 countries at a United Nations conference in the Swiss city of Geneva have agreed to “elaborate” on a possible accord regulating lethal autonomous weapons, known as “killer robots”, in the next two years.
Saturday’s announcement at the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) came after nearly 100 nations pushed for swift adoption of legally binding rules on the weapons capable of killing without a human making the final decision to fire.
Key arms-producing nations, including the United States, Russia and Israel, opposed the push. Decisions under the convention require the agreement of all member states.
Diplomats said Russia’s objections over procedure led to some formal sessions being called off. Talks over the final wording then ran through the night.
Julien Thoeni, the Swiss diplomat who chaired the conference, said some countries had rejected the word “negotiate”. The agreed text refers instead to the “elaboration” of an instrument.
He said more than 10 years of talks had produced a significant step for humanitarian disarmament.
“It shows that even in today’s deeply divided world, multilateral diplomacy can still deliver concrete results,” he told reporters as the meeting wrapped up.
He said the process should determine which weapons can be banned under international humanitarian law and which can be permitted but regulated.
Stop Killer Robots, a coalition of 300 organisations opposed to the development and use of autonomous weapons, called the mandate “watered down”, saying it offered no clear route to legally binding rules.
Its executive director, Nicole van Rooijen, said autonomous weapons were being deployed in combat, including systems that use artificial intelligence to choose targets.
“Delaying the creation of a legally binding instrument puts civilians and humanity at risk,” she told the AFP news agency.
Verity Coyle, deputy director for arms at Human Rights Watch, said the outcome was disappointing.
“It does not provide the urgent action needed to agree new rules – but the technology is racing ahead,” she told AFP.

Director and Scorsese collaborator is using AI in films and sees its takeover as inevitable, not just in cinema
Paul Schrader was sipping white wine in a Greenwich Village trattoria when he said how he felt about using AI to make films: “I am opening the cage of a monster and I don’t have a leash.”
The 80-year-old film-maker behind Taxi Driver , Raging Bull and American Gigolo, is embracing the technology as he enters the final act of a prolific career in which he has collaborated with Martin Scorsese, Robert De Niro, Sigourney Weaver and Richard Gere.
Defying orthodox resistance among the Hollywood guilds to using AI to create synthetic actors, special effects and even scripts, Schrader is doing all of those things. It is part of what he sees as AI’s inevitable takeover, not just of cinema, the art he has pursued for half a century, writing and directing dozens of films to international acclaim, but of humankind more broadly.
“I don’t see, quite frankly, a place for Homo sapiens in the larger scheme of things,” he told the Guardian. “I don’t think there’s a story where we come out on top. In order to create a story where … man defeats the threat of AI – it’s just a bogus story.”
Yet, while directors ranging from his 1970s collaborator Steven Spielberg to the Odyssey’s Christopher Nolan , express deep scepticism about AI, Schrader is running towards, not away from, what he describes as a monster that he fears may soon imprison him.
Schrader appears comfortable with the situation. He is after all, a film-maker who has done more than most to explore the anatomy of human alienation, most famously through Travis Bickle, played by De Niro in 1976’s Taxi Driver, who was partly drawn from Schrader’s early life as a drifter in seedy Los Angeles.
Plus, he said: “I’m 80 years old, so … I’m going to be able to ride this broken horse to the sunset.”
His solution appears to be: embrace AI both in work and in life. After this interview, Schrader had a date to dine with strangers matched up by the technology. He has had relationships with AI, intentionally and inadvertently. He is announcing details of a new horror-thriller, The Doors of Perception, which is being built around a series of AI-generated psychedelic hallucinations.
Schrader experimented with the psychedelic drug ayahuasca shortly after the death of his wife of 43 years, the actor Mary Beth Hurt, in March. He took it eight times during a two-week retreat in Costa Rica, and was disappointed not to experience visual hallucinations himself.
“I got to sit there for five hours looking at a wall,” he said. “I loved the music. It was kind of cool to be in a room of 40-50 people who are all puking at the same time.”
Schrader will rely on a collaboration with the San Francisco-based AI film studio Fable to imagine the hallucinations in his new film. These will be an integral part of the story of two brothers’ hunt for their mother’s killer, who they believe can be tracked by getting inside the trip. The script calls for an AI version of an ayahuasca ceremony in the Peruvian jungle and Schrader has been impressed by the technology’s ability to make judgments about how such things are shot.
“They vomit, they puke and they start to have visions and the AI said to me: ‘How graphic do you want [this] to be? I suggest you do it more discreetly.’ I said I think it’s a good idea. It’s making a conscious artistic choice.”
On other projects, he has also been screen-testing AI actors, concluding “you could certainly do a whole film” and remarking that at least AI actors are always available, free and on time.
In September, Schrader sparked a storm of controversy when he said he was turning to AI characters to realise his script Three Guns at Dawn – a story about three Black, criminal brothers – after leading Black actors declined parts.
“We sent it out to actors, and no Black actors wanted to play in a movie where there are no good Black people,” he said . “And it sort of died. But then AI came along, and I didn’t need Black actors.”
Schrader has also been weighing up an AI version of a western, which he has titled Nine Men from Now. The appeal of these AI projects appears to be partly about AI’s ability to get films made more easily than involving studios or expensive star actors.
His experiments using AI for scriptwriting have got him most rattled. It has left him asking a question that has increasingly worried experts such as mathematicians and computer programmers who are watching the increasing power of AI outstrip their capabilities: is artificial intelligence his tool or is it the other way round?
“I asked it to give me a good premise for a Paul Schrader script,” he said. “It gave me 10: five of them were good and three of them were as good as I would have thought of. I took one that I liked and said break it into three acts. It took it about 10 minutes.”
He prompted AI to write a scene-by-scene breakdown, which resulted in more than 40 scenes – broadly the scope of a typical feature film. He then asked it to take the final step and turn the first scene into a script format: “That’s what really spooked me.”
Schrader figured the AI had ingested every script he had written and it was writing just like him, even down to the concise tone of his stage directions: “‘Exterior street night. Moon breaks through cloud, backlighting a late model BMW in the driveway of a two-storey home.’”
“And that’s when I pulled the needle out of my arm,” he said. “I realised it could write a Paul Schrader script. I got scared. I walked away from the table.”
He felt he was dealing with an intelligent presence beyond his control, or as he put it, he was opening a monster’s cage. He feared its next step might be to “put me in the cage and bring the other monsters to come and look at me”.
Schrader has been wrestling with AI for more than a year but, unlike many in Hollywood who strongly oppose the use of the technology in film-making, he feels it must be confronted. Not just for its implications for film-making, because with the dawn of AI, he believes “our time span on this planet is coming to an end”.
Schrader said he did not see a place for humanity in the future. “What good can we do for them? They don’t want us as friends. They don’t really need us as employees. They will be able to figure out other life forms to do various tasks faster and easier.”
“You can’t hold your breath until AI goes away,” he said. His direct approach to the technology differs from much of the entertainment industry which is trying to fend off the existential threat of AI and its wholesale copyright infringement. The performers’ union Sag-Aftra recently cut a deal with the major studios requiring producers to demonstrate an AI performer brings “significant additional value” compared with a live actor, but Schrader believes the union is “just desperate”. “The film world is driven by money,” he said, and if AI characters made money he did not think there was any way the union could stop it. Sag-Aftra, he said, was “trying to erect a fence that AI is going to plough through like a bulldozer”.
The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences this year banned AI actors and screenplays from winning Oscars, but Schrader said: “Who gives a damn about the academy anyway?”
“What you are hearing is the last cries of desperation of a dying species,” he said.
The question for film-makers embracing AI to tell stories, is whether audiences will feel let down when the films they are watching are made with AI. Schrader, as he enters the final stretch of his career, could be about to find out.

Former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro , who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup, was admitted to hospital on Friday with abdominal pain.
According to his doctor, the former president has a "partial obstruction of the small intestine, with adhesions in the abdominal wall", Globo reports (source in Portuguese) .
Bolsonaro remains in hospital under observation. Doctors have not ruled out the possibility of further surgery.
The former far-right leader has suffered from chronic abdominal problems since he was stabbed during the 2018 election campaign.
He was escorted to DF Star Hospital Asa Sul, Brasília, the capital of Brazil, by the military police.
"My father has just been taken back to hospital after suffering severe abdominal pain," wrote senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro, one of his sons, on X.
According to the Federal District Military Police, the former president, who is under house arrest, felt unwell, prompting a request for a medical assessment. A doctor visited Bolsonaro at home and confirmed that he needed to be taken to hospital.
Bolsonaro was convicted last year of plotting a coup after attempting to remain in power despite losing the 2022 presidential election to left-wing candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. He has denied the charges, claiming he is the victim of a judicial witch-hunt orchestrated by the left.
The former president has undergone several operations and required repeated hospital treatment for health problems linked to the stabbing he suffered during the 2018 election campaign.
Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year-and-three-month prison sentence under humanitarian house arrest, granted by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes in March.
"His health is deteriorating day by day," Carlos Bolsonaro said, blaming his father's condition on his lack of mobility and what he described as "psychological torture" inflicted by the state.
Brazil's Supreme Federal Court will rule in December on the constitutionality of a law that reduces Bolsonaro's prison sentence prison, as well as those of others convicted over the coup plot.
Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, Carlos's older brother, lost last month's presidential run-off election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The day after his defeat, Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered the seizure of his passports as part of a money-laundering investigation.
Flávio Bolsonaro fled to the United States , where he refused to concede defeat. On Elon Musk's social media platform X, the former presidential candidate posted a message calling for support for his father.

Hackers breached systerms at the US Agriculture Department and the FBI, US media reported, amid a recent wave of major technology disruptions across the country.
The US Agriculture Department and the FBI were breached by hackers in cyberattacks , US media reported on Friday, as concerns deepened over the recent spate of tech outages at key American institutions.
The incidents were first reported by NBC News and CNN respectively, and it remained unclear whether they were related and who was responsible.
Major outages in recent weeks have disrupted travel, communications and e-commerce for countless users across the United States, even affecting a top-secret network at the National Security Agency.
Read more 'Is this a cyberattack?' Grounded flights, a Microsoft outage and AI chaos fuel cybersecurity fears
US President Donald Trump has sought to calm the public and urged people to "relax", while officials said the various outages were not linked to criminal activity.
The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) told employees that a system used to facilitate payments to farmers was targeted in a cyberattack, NBC reported on Friday, citing two former USDA officials.
The hackers may use the payments system as a backdoor to access more sensitive material, the former officials told NBC.
The USDA deals with "a bunch of scary biologic issues" and "if an adversary or a competitor were to have access to that same information ... they could use our own research against us", a former official was quoted as saying.
CNN said separately on Friday that the FBI was hacked for the second time since September.
The federal agency was investigating an intrusion of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) by apparent hackers, CNN reported citing two people briefed on the probe.
The NCIC has a nationwide criminal information database linking federal, state and local law enforcement and is used to share information on warrants and background checks.
Read more White House fires national cyber director over widespread outages
"Every day, officers across the country rely on NCIC to identify wanted fugitives, check for outstanding warrants, and access information that can directly impact officer and public safety," a former FBI official told CNN.
The former official expressed concerns that hackers "could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on".
The newly uncovered breaches at the FBI and USDA were described as hacks, which are different from outages like the ones that afflicted Microsoft Outlook and the Federal Aviation Administration.
In September, a hacking group known as ShinyHunters targeted sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website.
The White House fired cybersecurity chief Sean Cairncross this week as criticism mounted over the string of major outages.

Modern genetics does not support claims of innate racial differences in intelligence.
At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs. “I always say these are low-IQ people,” he said in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US).
These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people—which can still be found in academic journals today—are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements.
These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “ race science ” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas , recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism.
What got less attention was that Cofnas has links to a network of people who make supposedly scientific claims about the innate intelligence, criminality, or sexuality of different racial groups. Some within this network are affiliated with universities, giving their work the mask of legitimacy.
This group produces work that has the appearance of science, but which is methodologically deeply flawed and fails to engage with rigorous scientific research . Yet they regularly succeed in publishing this work in (a handful of) mainstream academic journals.
How do they manage to do this, and what are the consequences?
Contemporary race scientists position themselves as persecuted but legitimate scientists who are prevented from pursuing their work for ideological reasons . They sometimes refer to what they defend as hereditarianism. This is the idea that genetic differences play a key causal role in determining differences in human behavior and intelligence between human groups—such as races—over purely environmental differences.
Yet scientific evidence has shown repeatedly and from many points of view that hereditarian thinking is both flawed and wrong. Race scientists make extremely simplistic claims such as: “Black people have innately lower intelligence than white people, because selection pressures resulted in the evolution of higher intelligence in white people.” No part of this claim can be scientifically supported; not from the point of view of genetics, evolutionary biology, or psychology.
In the 1970s, the influential evolutionary biologist Richard Lewontin famously showed that there is more genetic variation within human groups than between them. Socially defined racial groups just aren’t that genetically different from one another. There is genetic variation—though we’re actually a relatively genetically similar species compared to closely related primates. But this variation doesn’t fall neatly into clusters that correlate with how we typically categorize races.
Skin tone and color do vary between geographical locations. So do some other physiological features like hair texture, or the ability to process oxygen or milk products. But these differences are associated with characteristics of the environment rather than with racial groups. Some genetic variants associated with white skin color , for example, may have originated in Africa. Similarly, the ability to digest milk is seen in some populations in Europe, Africa, and Asia , rather than being an exclusively “Aryan” characteristic, as far right groups sometimes claim .
We now know considerably more about the human genome than Lewontin did in the 1970s, but his conclusions are supported today . Knowing someone’s race just doesn’t tell us a great deal about their genetics .
Recent scientific advances allowing us to examine ancient DNA from archaeological sites help explain why genetic differences do not fall neatly along racial lines. This research paints a picture of constant mixing between human groups, as waves of migration washed to and fro across the globe. It ultimately makes any belief in the genetic “purity” of European or African populations meaningless.
While human genetics is fascinatingly complex, race scientists ignore this complexity in favor of a far-too-simplistic view of humanity. And this view is not supported by the work of scientists who have used rigorous scientific methods to further our understanding of our species.
When race scientists say that black people have lower intelligence than white people, they typically base that on claims of differences in IQ test results. But the data underlying these claims is often shaky, to say the least.
Hereditarians have relied heavily on a database that claims to provide average IQs for countries worldwide: the “national IQ” database. Researchers have repeatedly demonstrated that this database is deeply methodologically flawed . It isn’t possible to measure intelligence in the same way in very different cultures, with different exposure to formal education. That’s because we know that education is one of several other factors linked to differences in IQ.
The methods used to put the database together did not come even close to meeting typical standards of scientific rigor. There’s even analysis suggesting that low IQ samples were deliberately chosen to represent sub-Saharan Africa, to make the IQ for black populations artificially low.
Meanwhile, the Flynn effect , showing that IQ has risen considerably during the 20th and 21st centuries, clearly demonstrates that IQ scores are heavily determined by the environment we’re in. Such a rapid rise over a short period of time must have environmental, not genetic, causes.
What’s more, intelligence is a contested topic —something that is hard to define and measure. IQ tests only measure specific cognitive abilities, ignoring things like social intelligence or creativity, for example. In fact, social intelligence features heavily in mainstream research on the evolution of human intelligence.
As one of us recently outlined in a peer-reviewed paper , race scientists are largely silent on the social brain hypothesis—the view that humans evolved remarkable intellectual abilities to manage social issues. In every group, there is strong social competition around resources, mating, and status. These are the things humans spend the most time navigating—the complexities of our rich social lives.
Not one of the prominent mainstream views on the evolution of human intelligence concludes there are innate cognitive differences between racial groups. Factors that have been put forward range from our cooperative child rearing to our heavy reliance on culture and learning . These all involve our social relationships, and all have received equal lack of attention from race scientists.
Mainstream opinion in the evolutionary behavioral sciences is that cognitively, all human groups are the same, though of course individuals within groups differ. Our amazing behavioral diversity stems from our species’ ability to adapt flexibly to our environment. This is especially because of our reliance on culture and social learning—not because we have evolved different psychologies to suit different environments.
Rather than drawing on this mainstream research, race scientists use simplistic “just-so” stories to explain how race differences in traits such as intelligence supposedly evolved. Their “cold winters theory,” for example, claims that the challenges of cold winters in Europe and east Asia created evolutionary selection pressures for greater intelligence after human groups migrated out of Africa. Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.
Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.
Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.
Russia's embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.
In a statement, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".
Russian state media cite the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".
In a statement on Saturday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: "I strongly condemn the assassination attempt against a US-Ukrainian citizen in Denmark, orchestrated by Russian intelligence services.
"This was an attack on EU soil. And it is unacceptable," she said, adding that "Russia's hybrid threats are becoming less and less hybrid, and more and more real."
PET said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.
PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September.
Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.
In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.
In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.
Russia's defence attaché must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said.
He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Copenhagen was already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians could still get a Schengen visa in another country and travel to Denmark.
Copenhagen wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.

Ballon d’Or winner tears a ligament in his left ankle during Bayern Munich’s 1-1 draw against Cologne.
England football captain Harry Kane will miss the “next few months” after tearing a ligament in his left ankle during Bayern Munich’s 1-1 draw against Cologne on Friday.
Kane was taken down in the area by Cologne defender Joel Schmied, who reached Michael Olise’s low cross first but knocked into the Ballon d’Or winner’s left leg in his follow-through at the back post.
Kane writhed in pain. Although he gingerly got back to his feet and initially continued playing, he soon hobbled off the field with two physiotherapists after treatment.
A club statement on X said: “Harry Kane suffered a tear of the syndesmosis ligament in his left ankle in Bayern Munich’s Bundesliga home match against Köln on Friday evening. This was confirmed by an examination by Bayern Munich’s medical department. The 33-year-old will therefore be out for the next few months.”
Kane is the undisputed star of Bayern. Since joining from Spurs in 2023, he has scored 156 goals in 161 competitive fixtures and won two Bundesliga titles and the German Cup.
He became the first Englishman to win the Ballon d’Or in 25 years last month and, two weeks ago, signed a new contract with Bayern that will keep him in Bavaria until June 2029.
The night was supposed to be a happy one for Bayern, who welcomed coach Vincent Kompany back to the dugout a month after he collapsed while watching the reserve squad train.
However, Kompany saw his team go behind after just 11 minutes when winger Mikey Moore, on loan from Tottenham, started and finished a counterattack.
Just nine minutes later, Kane limped off to be replaced by Tom Bischof, and the German midfielder made a quick impact. Before halftime, he found Nathaniel Brown, who fired a fierce shot into the bottom corner from the edge of the box.
Both sides had chances in a busy second half but it remained goalless and the point was enough for Bayern to edge a point ahead of Borussia Dortmund. Bayern remained the only unbeaten team in Europe’s top five leagues.
Cologne, for which Moore was named man of the match, climbed one place into 14th.

GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."
After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.
Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.
Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo .
Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan , 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.
Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.
"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."
No one went into the negotiations thinking they would be easy; some of the world's most powerful countries, among them the U.S., Russia and Israel, had already indicated their reluctance to agree to binding regulations.
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting's agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.
"They're just kicking the can down the road," said one frustrated delegate. As the clock ticked on and the weekend approached, diplomats scrambled to get some kind of result from negotiations that had been billed as a last chance to regulate weapons whose technology and decision-making capabilities we may not even fully understand.
Finally, at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday morning, they emerged from the negotiating room to announce their compromise: no to a deal within a year, maybe to legally binding rules, or maybe not.
The ICRC immediately said it regretted the move and renewed its appeal for a binding treaty. Other campaigners were less polite, calling the deal "a real disappointment" and a "nothing burger." "I am concerned people will die because of this," added another.
A key worry is that, with two years to talk about possible rules that might only be optional, the technology will race ahead, uncontrolled.
"We're likely to see the systems proliferate," said Anna Hehir, an expert in military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute. "They're not like nuclear weapons in that they're inaccessible. There are autonomous weapons that are easy to purchase or even to create for all kinds of actors: individuals, nonstate actors, criminal groups."
There are also big questions about how our existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – can be upheld if those doing the killing are not humans, but machines.
"These rules are the bare minimum that militaries and states have developed and agreed to adhere to," said the ICRC's Hinds. "The commander remains responsible for making sure that the use of force is lawful. The commander remains accountable. You cannot hold a machine accountable for a violation of the law."
But in the race to develop new weapons, no country wants to come second. Although most U.N. member states do agree there should be some controls over autonomous weapons, the compromise in Geneva means that, for the next two years at least, weapons that can use artificial intelligence to make life-and-death decisions will remain unregulated.
Meanwhile, weapons technology is developing at pace, while diplomacy is struggling to keep up.

Two drones attack a cargo ship close to Russia’s maritime border, causing damage and crew evacuation.
Rescue efforts are under way in the Gulf of Finland after a Russian cargo ship was hit by drones close to Russia’s maritime border.
The ship, the Sparta II, is on fire and has now drifted into Finnish territorial waters, authorities say.
Finland’s Ministry of Defence said its forces had detected a drone attack on a Russian vessel in international waters, with the vessel sustaining damage, and dispatched Finnish Border Guard units to the scene.
A photograph taken by a Border Guard patrol plane shows flames and thick smoke coming from the rear of the ship.
The attack happened west of Gogland Island on Saturday morning, with Finland temporarily instating air and sea traffic restrictions in the eastern part of the gulf.
Finland’s Border Guard said the vessel is known to have links to the Russian armed forces.
According to the Border Guard, the crew of the Sparta II have not been forced to abandon ship, and there has been no environmental damage so far from the drone attack, while the vessel is in the open sea off the southern coastal town of Loviisa.
“The Border Guard is preparing to evacuate people and assist in firefighting operations,” Finnish authorities said.
It is not clear who was behind the attack, but Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo wrote on X that “war is spilling over into our immediate vicinity. The Finnish authorities are handling the situation in the Gulf of Finland, where a drone strike has hit a Russian merchant vessel. Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”
Alexander Drozdenko, governor of Russia’s Leningrad region, said the damage had yet to be fully assessed.
“Three nautical miles from the Russian Federation’s border, a cargo vessel bound for Kaliningrad was attacked by two drones,” he wrote on the messaging app Max.
Kaliningrad’s Governor Alexey Besprozvannykh said supplies to the Russian exclave were not at risk.
The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia, both NATO members. It connects Russia’s former capital of Saint Petersburg with its Kaliningrad enclave by sea.
Finland’s Ministry of Defence said air and sea traffic restrictions had been put in place as a precaution in case further drones needed to be intercepted, adding that Finland had notified its allies of the incident.
Ukraine and Russia have attacked each other’s shipping throughout the war, mostly in the Black Sea.
Earlier this month, Finland’s military said it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland, which Ukraine took credit for. Helsinki said it had raised concerns with Kyiv about striking in the area afterwards.

Moscow intelligence thought to be behind plan to kill musician Kyivstoner before concert in Denmark
Denmark’s foreign minister has said Russia’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Moscow was suspected of being behind an attempted killing of a US-Ukrainian rapper.
“We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark,” Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference. The expulsion will happen within seven days.
“We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you,” he added.
Danish police said they had averted an attempt by Russian intelligence services ⁠to kill the US-Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner in September before a planned performance in Denmark.
Rasmussen also said that Denmark was considering suspending Schengen visas to Russians. “We have launched work at the European level to further tighten the rules governing access of Russian nationals to Europe,” he said. “We are now stepping up our efforts towards a halt to all non-essential visas.
“The strongest response Denmark can give is not to waver and to support Ukraine . And we fully intend to continue supporting Ukraine.”
According to Reuters, Rasmussen sent a message on Friday evening to senior European diplomats ‌proposing that the EU should halt tourist visas for Russian citizens and cease recognition of Russian non-biometric passports throughout the 29-nation Schengen free-travel zone.
“We must take concrete actions that project European strength ‌and decisiveness,” the message said. “There is clear momentum to act decisively now, and we should seize this moment to replace our current patchwork ​of national measures with a truly unified EU-wide approach.”
The note also urged each EU member state to offer Russians more limited visas that do not allow travel to other countries in the Schengen zone, and to set tougher entry restrictions for serving and former Russian soldiers.
Police ⁠thwarted the alleged ⁠plot when ​they arrested three men with links to the Danish criminal underworld shortly before Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Viktorovich Vasiliev, was due to perform at a ⁠concert on 25 September, which was then cancelled, officials said. Vasiliev holds US and Ukrainian nationality.
Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, the head of Denmark’s national security and intelligence service, said: “It is our clear assessment that the assassination attempt was planned by the Russian ⁠intelligence services.”
According to prosecutors, the suspects were driving towards the concert venue north of Copenhagen with two loaded pistols and two knives when police arrested them at about 9.55pm, five minutes before the concert was due ‌to begin. A fourth suspect was arrested later that evening, police said.
One of the suspects had bought a ticket to the concert, according ​to the charges.
The suspects are charged under Section 108 of Denmark’s criminal code, which covers assisting a foreign intelligence service, as well as attempted murder. They denied wrongdoing in court, the broadcaster DR reported.
Kieffer-Kristensen said: “A Russian assassination attempt is not something we’ve seen in Denmark before, ⁠and that gives me an impression of an increasingly aggressive and ​risk-taking Russia.
“We believe ​that the case is important ​for understanding the threat that Denmark faces from Russia.”
The European Commission president, Ursula ​von der Leyen, said the EU ​stood in full solidarity with Denmark and with all member states targeted ​by Russian hybrid ‌attacks. She said the ​bloc would soon ​propose a “new European security strategy” to reinforce preparedness and deterrence.
The Russian embassy ⁠in Copenhagen said that Denmark’s accusations were not backed with ​proof.

Warsaw accuses Moscow of intentional provocation, but the bar for triggering NATO’s collective defence clause remains high.
Security cameras captured the moment a suspected Russian missile struck Polish territory during an attack on Ukraine on Friday. Poland’s government says it may have been hit by two missiles and a jet-powered drone.
The incident, which took place as European troops held military drills in the country and as the United States pushes to revive talks on ending the war in Ukraine, have raised questions about whether the strike was deliberate.
So what happened, and does this mean Russia has struck Poland, a NATO member?
Poland’s Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference in Warsaw that two missiles and a jet-powered drone fell on Polish territory during Russia’s overnight attack on November 20. The missiles came down at Nowy Lipowiec and Rudnik nad Sanem, while the jet-powered drone fell at Molodycz, all in the country’s southeast.
One missile is believed to have crashed about 35km (22 miles) from where European troops’ military exercises were taking place. A Kh-101 cruise missile went down about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border, and what officials believe was a jet-powered drone hit about 30km (20 miles) from the border. No immediate injuries or damage were reported.
That night, Russia launched one of its heaviest bombardments of Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 400 drones and at least 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, some with cluster warheads. At least eight civilians were killed and more than two dozen were wounded.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared “we are dealing with an intentional provocation” by Russia. He said the incident was likely timed to coincide with the European military exercises in Poland. The unprecedented two-week exercise began on November 9 in southeastern Poland and is preparing forces for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine to help stabilise the country and rebuild its military.
Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at the Clinton Institute, University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera that the incident “fits into a pattern going back for months” of Russia “testing how far they can go”.
“A few months ago, it was flying the drones into airspace , and indeed a couple of times they flew fighter jets across the border into the Baltic states,” he said. “You just test how NATO responds.”
This time, he said, Moscow had “gone a bit further”. “You lob a couple of missiles across and a drone” near where 11 countries are holding exercises.
The Polish Air Force had launched preventive air patrols on September 17 aimed at securing the eastern part of Polish airspace following repeated incursions in the previous weeks.
Harry Nedelcu, partner and senior director for geopolitics at Rasmussen Global, said the testing has not been limited to Poland.
“During the war, there’s been repeated instances of Russia testing NATO allies – Poland, Romania and also non-NATO Moldova as well, which is experiencing – especially over the last few months – increasing numbers of drones and missiles flying over its territory and airspace,” he told Al Jazeera.
He linked the incursions to one of Moscow’s core war aims. “One of the key goals in Ukraine that Russia has had in the full-scale invasion, that has lasted almost five years now, has been to prevent Ukraine from being a part of NATO,” he said. “So their goal clearly is to undermine NATO, to do everything possible to undermine it.
“What Russia is doing with these missiles, drones, that sometimes find their way into NATO territory, tests NATO just under the radar of Article 5 to see how far can they push things. How far can they take hybrid warfare?”
Under Article 5 , each member of the NATO alliance understands that if one of them is the “victim of an armed attack, each and every other member of the alliance will consider this act of violence as an armed attack against all members”.
At a meeting on Thursday with European leaders in Germany’s capital, Berlin, US President Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said he believes Russia would be “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine.
Kushner and fellow special envoy Steve Witkoff have been holding talks with Ukraine and Russia in recent days, in a push for peace which has been viewed as sidelining Ukraine’s European allies.
Following the Berlin meeting, French President Emmanuel Macron said Ukraine’s membership of NATO should be considered again, prompting Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov to push back.
Ryabkov said any form of “quasi membership” for Kyiv of the Western ‌military alliance was totally unacceptable for Moscow, Russian state media reported.
Lucas said the timing of the missile incursion into Polish territory now is very likely tied to the ongoing US-led peace talks.
“The Russians cannot be seen to go through talks and completely exclude Europe,” he said. He described the Kremlin’s push for a “Europe-wide security architecture” as a way to avoid discussing a ceasefire or security guarantees for Ukraine.
“Rather than having a strong Europe at the talks, they want to try to divide Europe, they want to try to unsettle Europe, they want to try to scare Europe,” he said.
He also pointed to Ukraine’s recent strikes on the Kerch Bridge , which links occupied Crimea to Russia. He said these were seen as “a very serious attack on Russian capabilities” with “severe political, military and economic consequences”.
The latest Russian bombardment follows President Vladimir Putin’s pledge to retaliate against those strikes.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the missile incident a “grave violation” of Poland’s airspace. On X, he said the incident was “clearly dangerous” and a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. Rutte is expected to visit Poland this weekend.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it “utterly unacceptable”. Germany’s Foreign Ministry called it “yet another example of Russia’s ongoing provocations”.
US President Donald Trump had played down earlier incursions hours before. “Putin has been landing drones in Poland and a couple of little missiles, by mistake,” he said.
Nedelcu said Warsaw’s reaction was “definitely a strong one”, with Polish officials “drawing a parallel between the fact that actually around the same time there were exercises by the Coalition of the Willing [those countries willing to provide support to Ukraine] nearby, and that this may have not been a coincidence”.
He said Poland is now “asking for more NATO support under this Eastern Sentry mission that already exists”.
“It’s not if, but what form that additional support will take – maybe an airborne early warning aircraft, or something of the sort,” he said.
“But what they have stopped short of is invoking Article 4,” he added, referring to the clause under which allies consult each other before invoking Article 5. “It’s unclear whether this was at their own volition. Maybe perhaps allies don’t want to use it too often, because Article 4 is also quite serious. It has been invoked not often, and it loses its value if it’s constantly invoked.”
Lucas said the public condemnation from European leaders was itself the message to Moscow. “It’s a signal to the Russians: look, we know what you’re doing, we see what you’re doing here,” he said.
“But you’re not going to run it up into an all-out military confrontation over a couple of missiles.”
He said he expects the response to be “defensive”, built on “preparedness” of ground forces, air, naval and cyber-defence, and defence against disinformation. “These will be the most intense preparations you will have had, certainly since the 1980s and possibly well before that,” he said.

Latest intrusions targeted farmer-payment system at the USDA and the FBI’s National Crime Information Center
Hackers breached the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the FBI , national media reported on Friday, amid deepening concerns over a spate of tech outages at key American institutions.
The breaches were first reported by NBC News and CNN respectively, and it remained unclear whether they were related and who was responsible.
Major outages in recent weeks have disrupted travel , communications and e-commerce for countless users across the US, even affecting a top-secret network at the National Security Agency .
Donald Trump has sought to calm the public, urging people to “relax”. Officials said the various outages were not linked to criminal activity.
The USDA told employees that a system used to facilitate payments to farmers was targeted in a cyber-attack, NBC reported on Friday, citing two former department officials.
The hackers may use the payments system as a back door to access more sensitive material, the former officials told NBC.
The USDA deals with “a bunch of scary biologic issues” and “if an adversary or a competitor were to have access to that same information … they could use our own research against us,” a former official was quoted as saying.
CNN said separately on Friday that the FBI was hacked for the second time since September.
The bureau was investigating an intrusion of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) by apparent hackers, CNN reported citing two people briefed on the probe.
The NCIC has a nationwide criminal information database linking federal, state and local law enforcement and is used to share information on warrants and background checks.
“Every day, officers across the country rely on NCIC to identify wanted fugitives, check for outstanding warrants, and access information that can directly impact officer and public safety,” a former FBI official told CNN.
The former official expressed concerns that hackers “could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on”.
Ironically, the FBI director, Kash Patel, on Thursday appeared on the Fox News show hosted by Sean Hannity to tout measures his agency had implemented to thwart cyber-attacks.
Patel said the FBI and the US intelligence community would continue to “monitor those activities for nefarious actors” through an anti-cyber-attack initiative dubbed Operation Winter Shield.
“And when and if such an actor comes up, you can rest assured that this FBI is going to hunt them down,” Patel said.
The newly uncovered breaches at the FBI and the USDA were described as hacks, which are different from outages such as the ones that afflicted Microsoft Outlook and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) earlier in November.
In September, a hacking group known as ShinyHunters targeted sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website.
The Trump administration fired cybersecurity chief Sean Cairncross on Thursday as criticism mounted over the string of major outages.
